photos.caption: The living room, built around the boulder of the hearth.
photos.credit: Photo: Sakul9 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was a weekend house for the owner of a Pittsburgh department store and his wife.
Its terraces cantilever out over a waterfall.
Its architect also designed a spiral museum in New York.

summary.description: Frank Lloyd Wright designed this weekend house in 1934 for Edgar and Liliane Kaufmann, who owned a Pittsburgh department store, and built it directly over a waterfall on Bear Run. Reinforced-concrete terraces cantilever out from a stone core above the falls; the family moved in in 1937, and a guest wing followed in 1939.
keyFeatures: Stone chimney core rising from the rock
Bands of glass opening to the woods
funFacts: It has been open to visitors since 1963, run by the Western Pennsylvania Conservancy.
It is part of the UNESCO site 'The 20th-Century Architecture of Frank Lloyd Wright'.

architects.name: Jørn Utzon
architects.bio: Utzon won the 1957 competition for the Opera House with a design that made his name, but resigned in 1966 amid disputes over cost and design. He received the Pritzker Prize in 2003.

architects.name: Peter Hall
architects.bio: Australian architect who led the team that completed the Opera House, including its interiors, after Utzon's resignation.

photos.alt: White sail-like shells on a podium by a harbour, with skyscrapers behind
photos.credit: Photo: Bengt Nyman · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Large concert hall with wooden ceiling panels, tiers of seats and a stage
photos.caption: The concert hall.
photos.credit: Photo: PLBechly · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Its architect won an international competition of 233 entries in 1957, but left before it was finished.
Its roof shells are covered in over a million tiles.
It stands on a point jutting into a harbour.

summary.description: Jørn Utzon won the 1955–57 competition with a design of white concrete 'shells' rising from a monumental podium on Bennelong Point. After disputes over cost and design he resigned in 1966, and an Australian team led by Peter Hall completed the building, which Queen Elizabeth II opened on 20 October 1973.
keyFeatures: Roof 'shells' cut from a sphere of 75.2 m radius
1,056,006 glossy white and matte cream tiles
Monumental podium clad in pink granite
Glass walls closing the shells' open ends
funFacts: The shells are actually precast concrete panels on precast ribs, not shells in the structural sense.
It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2007.
The competition drew 233 entries from 32 countries.

architects.name: Rafael da Silva e Castro
architects.bio: Portuguese architect who designed the Cabinet's headquarters in the Neo-Manueline style, evoking the architecture of Portugal's Age of Discovery.

photos.alt: Ornate pale stone façade with pointed arches and pinnacles, at the end of a cobbled street
photos.credit: Photo: Estela Neto · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Tall reading room lined with tiers of wooden bookcases under a decorated skylight
photos.caption: The main reading room.
photos.credit: Photo: Rodrigo.Argenton · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was founded in 1837 by Portuguese immigrants, many of them political refugees.
Its style revives the ornate architecture of Portugal's Age of Discovery.
Its façade stone was carved in Lisbon and shipped across the Atlantic.

summary.description: Founded in 1837 by Portuguese immigrants in the then capital of the Empire of Brazil, the Cabinet built its headquarters in 1880–87 to a design by Rafael da Silva e Castro. Its Neo-Manueline style recalls the late Gothic of Portugal's Age of Discovery, and its reading room is lined floor to ceiling with carved bookcases beneath a skylight.
keyFeatures: Neo-Manueline façade inspired by the Jerónimos Monastery in Lisbon
Façade stone carved in Lisbon and shipped to Rio
Reading room with tiers of carved wooden bookcases
funFacts: Emperor Pedro II laid the cornerstone on 10 June 1880.
Princess Isabel inaugurated the building on 10 September 1887.
Statues on the façade portray figures such as Pedro Álvares Cabral and Luís de Camões.

architects.name: Celestial Sacardim
architects.bio: Italian architect under whom construction of the Manaus opera house began in 1884.

photos.alt: Pink and white theatre with a columned portico under a colourful tiled dome, at dusk
photos.credit: Photo: Periclesd · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Horseshoe auditorium with tiers of gilded boxes facing a stage
photos.caption: The auditorium.
photos.credit: Photo: gabriel_srsmith · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built in the middle of a rainforest at the height of a rubber boom.
Its roof tiles came from Alsace, its steel walls from Glasgow and its marble from Carrara.
It opened on the last day of 1896; the first opera was performed a week later.

summary.description: Built during the Belle Époque, when the rubber trade made Manaus one of the richest cities in Brazil, this opera house was inaugurated on 31 December 1896. Almost everything was imported: roof tiles from Alsace, steel walls from Glasgow, Carrara marble from Italy. Its dome is covered in 36,000 ceramic tiles in the colours of the Brazilian flag.
keyFeatures: Dome clad in 36,000 tiles in the national colours
Ceiling panels painted by Domenico de Angelis
198 chandeliers, 32 of them in Murano glass
funFacts: The first performance, on 7 January 1897, was Ponchielli's opera La Gioconda.

architects.name: José Tibúrcio Pereira de Magalhães
architects.bio: Engineer and architect from Recife who planned the theatre in Belém.

photos.alt: Salmon-coloured façade with white columns, portrait medallions and arched openings
photos.credit: Photo: Celso  Abreu · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Red and gold auditorium with tiers of boxes facing a stage curtain
photos.caption: The auditorium.
photos.credit: Photo: Pedro Matheus Ferreira Brito · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built during the golden age of rubber in the Amazon basin.
Its name was suggested by a bishop, who also laid its foundation stone in 1869.
It stands on a square named after the Republic in a city at the mouth of the Amazon.

summary.description: Built between 1869 and 1874 during the Amazon rubber boom, Belém's theatre follows strict neoclassical lines, with colonnaded patios on each side opening onto the Praça da República. After an administrative investigation it finally opened in February 1878, and the world's great opera companies performed there until the boom ended.
keyFeatures: Side patios with columns and staircases
Horseshoe auditorium with tiers of boxes
Fewer columns over the entrance than originally built
funFacts: Its first production, on 16 February 1878, was the drama The Two Orphans.
It was neglected after the rubber boom collapsed, and later restored.

name: Estação da Luz
aliases: Estação da Luz de São Paulo

architects.name: Charles Henry Driver
architects.bio: Victorian architect known for his pioneering use of ornamental ironwork, who designed the station for the London-based São Paulo Railway.

photos.alt: Long cream and red brick building with steep slate roofs and a clock tower
photos.credit: Photo: Marcos Elias de Oliveira Júnior · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Train platforms under a long arched roof of iron and glass
photos.caption: The train shed.
photos.credit: Photo: LUIZ CARLOS FERNANDES MELO JUNIOR · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was designed in Britain for a railway company based in London.
Its clock tower once set the time for the whole city.
It now also houses a museum of a language.

summary.description: Designed by the British architect Charles Henry Driver for the São Paulo Railway, which linked the port of Santos to the interior, the station was built in 1895–1901. Its iron and glass train shed and its brick and stone headquarters with a tall clock tower brought Victorian Britain to São Paulo.
keyFeatures: Clock tower that once regulated city time
Brick and stone façade with steep slate roofs
funFacts: A fire in 1946 destroyed the tower, which was rebuilt five years later.
The Museum of the Portuguese Language opened inside it in 2006; a fire in 2015 badly damaged the building.

architects.name: Adolfo del Vecchio
architects.bio: Engineer and director of works at Brazil's Ministry of Finance, who designed the customs post in a Gothic style inspired by Viollet-le-Duc.

photos.alt: Small green neo-Gothic castle with a pointed tower on an island in a bay
photos.credit: Photo: Clarissa Sá · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Painted blue vault with ribs meeting at a lantern
photos.caption: A painted vault inside the tower.
photos.credit: Photo: Andrevruas · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built as a customs post on a small island in a bay.
It hosted the last great ball of an empire, six days before the empire fell.
Its style was inspired by the French restorer of Gothic cathedrals, Viollet-le-Duc.

summary.description: Built on a small island in Guanabara Bay for the customs service of the port of Rio de Janeiro, this little Neo-Gothic 'château' was inaugurated by Emperor Pedro II on 27 April 1889. On 9 November it hosted the Ilha Fiscal Ball, remembered as the last ball of the Empire: six days later the Republic was proclaimed.
keyFeatures: Neo-Gothic silhouette of spires and battlements
Tower clock lit from inside for ships at night
Wings aligned east–west, pointing out the shipping channel
funFacts: Legend says that after the ball, bodices, corsets and garters were found all over the island.
It now belongs to the Brazilian Navy and has been restored since 2001.

name: Catedral da Sé de São Paulo

architects.name: Maximilian Emil Hehl
architects.bio: German engineer and architect from Kassel who emigrated to Brazil in 1888, taught in São Paulo and designed the new cathedral in a Gothic Revival style.

drawings.label: Façade design (project)
drawings.alt: Gothic Revival cathedral front with two tall spires, a rose window and a central gable
drawings.credit: Maximilian Emil Hehl, project drawing · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Grey stone Gothic Revival cathedral with tall towers, seen from below
photos.credit: Photo: Photograph by Mike Peel · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Long Gothic nave with clustered columns and pointed vaults
photos.caption: The nave.
photos.credit: Photo: Paul R. Burley · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It is a Gothic Revival cathedral crowned by a Renaissance-style dome.
It took four decades to build and was inaugurated for its city's fourth centenary.
Its crypt holds the remains of an 18th-century pioneer of airships.

summary.description: Begun in 1913 on the site of the demolished colonial cathedral, to designs by Maximilian Emil Hehl, the Sé is a five-aisled Gothic Revival church with a dome inspired by Florence. It was inaugurated in 1954 for São Paulo's fourth centenary, with its towers still unfinished; they were completed in 1967.
keyFeatures: Renaissance-style dome 30 metres over the crossing
Large crypt beneath the main altar
funFacts: It holds up to 8,000 people.
The remains of the airship pioneer Bartolomeu de Gusmão were moved to its crypt in 2004.

architects.name: Tommaso Gaudenzio Bezzi
architects.bio: Turin-born engineer and architect who settled in Brazil in 1875 and worked for the imperial court; the Ipiranga monument-building is his best-known work.

photos.alt: Long ochre palace with a columned central pavilion behind gardens and palm trees
photos.credit: Photo: Arimart · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Looking up through a gilded stair hall to a coffered skylight
photos.caption: The grand stair hall.
photos.credit: Photo: Ministério da Ciência, Tecnologia e Inovação · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built as a monument on the spot where a country's independence was proclaimed.
Its most famous painting shows a prince on horseback raising his sword.
It reopened in 2022 after nine years of restoration, for an independence bicentenary.

summary.description: Designed in 1884 by Tommaso Gaudenzio Bezzi as a monument to Brazilian independence, on the banks of the Ipiranga brook where Pedro I is said to have declared it in 1822, this palatial building opened as a museum in 1895. It houses Pedro Américo's painting Independence or Death and reopened in 2022 after a long restoration.
keyFeatures: Palatial façade with a columned central pavilion
Formal gardens and fountains on the axis
Built as a monument before becoming a museum
funFacts: It opened on 7 September 1895, Independence Day.
It is the oldest public museum in São Paulo and belongs to the University of São Paulo.

architects.name: Charles Garnier
architects.bio: A relatively unknown architect when he won the 1861 competition for the new Paris opera, Garnier went on to design the Opéra de Monte-Carlo. His opulent opera became the emblem of the Second Empire's style.

drawings.label: Main floor plan (1875)
drawings.alt: Symmetrical plan of a huge theatre: a horseshoe auditorium, a deep stage, and grand foyers and stairs at the front
drawings.credit: Charles Garnier · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

drawings.label: Section through the auditorium
drawings.alt: Coloured section through a horseshoe auditorium with tiers of red boxes under a painted dome
drawings.credit: Charles Garnier · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Ornate domed theatre with a green copper dome and gilded statues, seen over Paris rooftops
photos.credit: Photo: Alvesgaspar · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Grand marble staircase dividing into two flights beneath tiers of balconies
photos.caption: The Grand Staircase.
photos.credit: Photo: Benh LIEU SONG · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was commissioned by an emperor and won in a competition by a little-known architect.
A water tank beneath its stage inspired the lake in a famous novel and musical.
Its auditorium ceiling was repainted in 1964 by Marc Chagall.

summary.description: Built for the Paris Opera between 1861 and 1875 at the behest of Napoleon III, Charles Garnier's opera house blends Baroque, Palladian and Renaissance sources over an iron frame, leaving no surface undecorated. Its grand marble staircase, gilded foyer and horseshoe auditorium made it the emblem of Second Empire Paris.
keyFeatures: Grand Staircase of white marble with red and green balustrades
Concrete cistern under the stage holding groundwater
funFacts: The underground water tank inspired the lake in Gaston Leroux's The Phantom of the Opera.
Garnier beat Viollet-le-Duc, the Empress's favourite, in the competition.
Marc Chagall's 1964 ceiling is mounted on a removable frame over the original.

architects.name: Lluís Domènech i Montaner
architects.bio: Barcelona architect and politician, one of the leading figures of Catalan Modernisme. His buildings, including the Palau and the Hospital de Sant Pau, combine exposed brick and iron with mosaic, ceramics and stained glass.

photos.alt: Corner façade of red brick, mosaic and sculpted columns above arched entrances on a narrow street
photos.credit: Photo: Thomas Ledl · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Concert hall under an inverted stained-glass dome, with tiers of seats and stained-glass walls
photos.caption: The concert hall and its inverted skylight.
photos.credit: Photo: Thomas Ledl · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built for a choral society that led a revival of its region's culture.
Its concert hall is said to be the only one in Europe lit entirely by daylight.
Its architect also designed a nearby hospital listed with it as a World Heritage Site.

summary.description: Built in 1905–08 for the Orfeó Català choral society, Domènech i Montaner's concert hall wraps a light-filled auditorium of about 2,200 seats in exposed brick, iron, mosaic and stained glass. During the day it is lit entirely by natural light, through stained-glass walls and a skylight whose centrepiece is an inverted golden dome.
keyFeatures: Inverted stained-glass dome by Antoni Rigalt
Exposed brick and iron with mosaic and tile
funFacts: It was inaugurated on 9 February 1908.
It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997, together with the Hospital de Sant Pau.
The large mosaic at the top of the façade is impossible to see clearly from the narrow street below.

architects.name: Otto Wagner
architects.bio: Viennese architect, designer and urban planner, a leading member of the Vienna Secession. This bank is his best-known building.

drawings.label: Raised ground floor plan
drawings.alt: Plan of a trapezoid block around courtyards, with a large central hall
drawings.credit: Otto Wagner · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

drawings.label: Section through the banking hall
drawings.alt: Section of a hall under a curved glass roof with thin columns and suspended rods
drawings.credit: Otto Wagner · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Façade of square marble panels studded with metal bolts, above a canopied entrance
photos.credit: Photo: GFreihalter · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Banking hall under a curved glass roof on slender columns, with a glass floor
photos.caption: The banking hall (Kassenhalle).
photos.credit: Photo: GFreihalter · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built in 1904–06 with what was then a completely new material: reinforced concrete.
The bolts on its marble façade became a famous feature of its design.
Its architect used aluminium for columns, statues and even the heating blowers.

summary.description: Built in 1904–06 for the imperial postal savings bank, Otto Wagner's building faces its square with thin marble slabs fixed by aluminium-capped bolts. Inside, the banking hall sits under a curved glass roof on slender columns, with a glass floor that lights the rooms below and aluminium hot-air blowers standing like sculptures.
keyFeatures: Glass-roofed banking hall with a glass floor
Aluminium columns, statues and heating blowers
funFacts: Its cast-aluminium rooftop statues by Othmar Schimkowitz were among the first of their kind.
For years the bolts were thought decorative; analysis showed they really hold the marble slabs.
It was extended in 1910–12.

architects.name: Frank Lloyd Wright
architects.bio: Over a career of some seventy years Wright developed an 'organic architecture' rooted in landscape, from the Prairie houses of the 1900s to Fallingwater. The Guggenheim was his only museum, completed months after his death.

photos.alt: Curving white spiral building widening as it rises, on a city street corner
photos.credit: Photo: Bmzuckerman · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Looking up a white spiral ramp around an atrium towards a glass skylight
photos.caption: The spiral atrium.
photos.credit: Photo: Bmzuckerman · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It took 15 years to design and build, and opened in 1959.
Its galleries line a continuous six-storey ramp around a skylit atrium.
It is the only museum its architect ever designed.

summary.description: Commissioned in 1943 for Solomon R. Guggenheim's art collection, Frank Lloyd Wright's museum on Fifth Avenue took 15 years to design and build. Instead of rooms, visitors follow a continuous spiral ramp that widens as it rises around a central atrium lit by a skylight.
keyFeatures: Helical ramp gallery around an open atrium
Spiral that widens as it rises
funFacts: The collection's curator, Hilla Rebay, at first thought the 76-year-old Wright was dead.
Wright produced four different designs in 1943–44.
It is part of the UNESCO site 'The 20th-Century Architecture of Frank Lloyd Wright'.

architects.name: William Van Alen
architects.bio: American architect best known for designing the Chrysler Building in 1928–30.

photos.alt: Skyscraper with a tapering, terraced stainless-steel crown, seen from the street between towers
photos.credit: Photo: PortableNYCTours · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Lobby with marble walls, an inlaid ceiling and Art Deco lamps
photos.caption: The triangular lobby.
photos.credit: Photo: Tony Hisgett · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was briefly the tallest building in the world, for 11 months after its completion in 1930.
Its corners carry steel ornaments shaped like car radiator caps and eagles.
It was built for a car manufacturer, as an investment for his children rather than as company headquarters.

summary.description: Commissioned by the car maker Walter Chrysler and designed by William Van Alen, this 319-metre Art Deco skyscraper won a race with 40 Wall Street to become the tallest building in the world in 1930, before the Empire State Building overtook it. Its terraced stainless-steel crown and its gargoyles of radiator caps and eagles made it an icon of New York.
keyFeatures: Terraced crown with triangular windows and a spire
Steel ornaments of radiator caps and eagles
Triangular lobby of marble and inlaid wood
Tallest steel-framed brick building in the world
funFacts: It was the world's first supertall skyscraper.
It was never the headquarters of the Chrysler Corporation, which stayed in Detroit.

architects.name: Mimar Sinan
architects.bio: Chief architect to the Ottoman sultans for some fifty years, Sinan was also an engineer and mathematician, and his mosques defined classical Ottoman architecture.

drawings.label: Plan at the level of the domes
drawings.alt: Plan of a square prayer hall under a great central dome flanked by half-domes and smaller domes
drawings.credit: Cornelius Gurlitt, drawing, 1912 · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Courtyard arcade with small domes in front of a mosque with a great central dome
photos.credit: Photo: Dursun Sülük · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Vast prayer hall under a central dome with rings of windows and hanging lamps
photos.caption: Under the central dome.
photos.credit: Photo: Giorgio Galeotti · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built for a sultan known as 'the Magnificent'.
Its designer was the greatest architect of his empire, working for some fifty years.
Its patron sought to rival a famous 6th-century domed church in the same city.

summary.description: Commissioned by Suleiman the Magnificent and designed by the imperial architect Mimar Sinan, the mosque was founded in 1550 and inaugurated in 1557 on the Third Hill above the Golden Horn. Its great dome on half-domes answers the Hagia Sophia. Suleiman and his wife Hürrem are buried in tombs behind it.
keyFeatures: Central dome carried on two half-domes
Rings of windows lighting the prayer hall
Tombs of Suleiman and Hürrem Sultan behind the qibla wall
funFacts: Part of the dome collapsed in the earthquake of 1766.
Recent cleaning showed Sinan experimented with blue before making red the dome's main colour.

architects.name: Christopher Wren
architects.bio: Astronomer and mathematician turned architect, Wren led the rebuilding of London's churches after the Great Fire of 1666. St Paul's is his masterpiece, and he is buried in its crypt.

drawings.label: Plan (18th-century engraving)
drawings.alt: Cross-shaped cathedral plan with a large domed crossing and rounded transept ends
drawings.credit: Remi Parr, engraving · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Great domed cathedral with a lantern on top, seen across a square
photos.credit: Photo: Jumk18 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Looking up into a painted dome above the crossing, with gilded arches
photos.caption: The crossing beneath the inner dome.
photos.credit: Photo: Rachelle Haun · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It replaced a Gothic cathedral destroyed in a great fire in 1666.
Its dome is really three: an inner dome, a hidden brick cone, and an outer shell.
A gallery inside its dome carries a whisper from one side to the other.

summary.description: Begun in 1675 after the Great Fire of London gutted the old Gothic cathedral, Christopher Wren's English Baroque church was completed in 1710. Its dome, 111 metres high, made it the tallest building in London until 1963: a brick cone hidden between an inner dome and an outer shell carries the stone lantern.
keyFeatures: Triple-shell dome with a hidden brick cone
Whispering Gallery around the base of the dome
Crypt with the tombs of Wren, Nelson and Wellington
funFacts: Wren's epitaph reads: 'Reader, if you seek his monument, look around you.'
The date of its first stone is disputed: different accounts give 21, 25 and 28 June 1675.

architects.name: Gian Lorenzo Bernini
architects.bio: The dominant artist of Baroque Rome, Bernini was sculptor, architect and painter at once, a universal artist in the Renaissance sense.

drawings.label: Façade and plan (c. 1700)
drawings.alt: Elevation of a church front with a pediment on two pilasters and a semicircular porch, with its plan below
drawings.credit: Domenico de Rossi, engraving · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Church front with a tall pediment on pilasters and a curved porch on two columns, above wide steps
photos.credit: Photo: Gunnar Klack · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Gilded coffered oval dome with a lantern and figures on the cornice
photos.caption: The oval dome above the nave.
photos.credit: Photo: Cm9462 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built for a seminary of the Jesuits.
Its main space is an oval entered across its shorter axis.
Its architect called it one of his most perfect works and liked to sit inside it in old age.

summary.description: Designed by Gian Lorenzo Bernini for the Jesuit novitiate on the Quirinal Hill, the church was built in 1658–61 and decorated until 1670. Its oval nave is entered across the short side, so the eye goes straight to the altar, where the story of Saint Andrew's martyrdom rises from painting to a sculpted saint and on into the golden dome.
keyFeatures: Oval plan entered on its short axis
funFacts: It was commissioned by Cardinal Camillo Pamphili with the approval of Pope Alexander VII.
It holds the tomb of King Charles Emmanuel IV of Sardinia, who became a Jesuit.

architects.name: Balthasar Neumann
architects.bio: Military engineer and court architect to the prince-bishops of Würzburg, Neumann was one of the greatest designers of late Baroque Central Europe.

drawings.label: Main floor plan
drawings.alt: Plan of a vast palace around several courtyards, with an oval hall projecting at the centre
drawings.credit: Felix Mader, drawing · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

drawings.label: Section through the staircase and halls
drawings.alt: Section through a grand staircase under a wide vault, next to two halls
drawings.credit: Felix Mader, drawing · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Long palace with a central pavilion, seen across a formal garden
photos.credit: Photo: Derzno · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Grand staircase rising beneath a vast painted ceiling
photos.caption: The staircase and Tiepolo's ceiling.
photos.credit: Photo: Graham Fellows · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built for prince-bishops and is said to have been called 'the largest parsonage in Europe' by Napoleon.
Its staircase is covered by the largest continuous ceiling fresco in the world, painted by a Venetian master.
Its central halls survived a 1945 air raid that burned out the rest of the building.

summary.description: Begun in 1720 for the Schönborn prince-bishops of Würzburg and completed in 1744, Balthasar Neumann's palace is one of Germany's great Baroque residences. Its staircase rises under an unsupported vault painted in 1752–53 by Giovanni Battista Tiepolo with the four continents, the largest continuous ceiling fresco in the world.
keyFeatures: Grand staircase under an unsupported vault
Tiepolo's fresco of the four continents
funFacts: It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1981.
Neumann died in 1753, the year Tiepolo finished the staircase fresco.

architects.name: Mestre Roberto
architects.bio: A 12th-century master builder, probably from northern Europe, who was also directing the construction of Lisbon Cathedral and to whom the design of Coimbra's cathedral is attributed.

architects.name: Mestre Bernardo
architects.bio: Master builder who supervised the works of Coimbra's cathedral, succeeded by Master Soeiro.

photos.alt: Fortress-like stone church front with crenellated walls and a deep arched portal
photos.credit: Photo: Berthold Werner · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Romanesque nave with round arches leading to a gilded Gothic altarpiece
photos.caption: The nave.
photos.credit: Photo: thirdsphoto · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was begun after its city became the capital of a newly declared kingdom in the 12th century.
From outside it looks like a small fortress, with crenellated walls and few, narrow windows.
It is the only cathedral of its kind from the Reconquista to survive relatively intact in its country.

summary.description: Begun after King Afonso Henriques made Coimbra the capital of the new kingdom of Portugal, the cathedral was largely complete in the early 13th century. Its design is attributed to Master Robert and its works to Master Bernard. With its crenellated walls and narrow windows it looks like a fortress, and it is the only Portuguese Romanesque cathedral of the Reconquista to survive relatively intact.
keyFeatures: Deep portal and window with Romanesque carving
funFacts: Its cloister was begun only in 1218, under King Afonso II.
In 1772 the bishop's seat moved to the former Jesuit church, now the New Cathedral.

name: Mosteiro da Batalha
aliases: Mosteiro de Santa Maria da Vitória
Monastery of Saint Mary of the Victory

architects.name: Afonso Domingues
architects.bio: Lisbon-born master builder who drew the original design of the monastery and directed its works from 1388 until his death.

architects.name: David Huguet
architects.bio: Master builder who succeeded Afonso Domingues in 1402 and directed the works until 1438, raising the nave and building the Founder's Chapel and the chapter house.

drawings.label: General plan
drawings.alt: Plan of a long church with an octagonal chapel at its head and large cloisters beside it
drawings.credit: From 'Monumentos de Portugal' (1886) · No restrictions · Wikimedia Commons

drawings.label: Longitudinal section of the church
drawings.alt: Section of a tall Gothic church with pointed windows, pinnacles and a spire
drawings.credit: James Murphy, engraving, 1793 · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Ornate Gothic church with pinnacles, flying buttresses and tall traceried windows
photos.credit: Photo: Alvesgaspar · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Very tall, narrow Gothic nave with coloured light falling on its piers
photos.caption: The nave.
photos.credit: Photo: Ray Swi-hymn · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built to give thanks for a victory over Castile in 1385.
It took more than a century to build, spanning the reigns of seven kings.
Its 'Unfinished Chapels' were never roofed.

summary.description: Officially the Monastery of Saint Mary of the Victory, Batalha fulfilled King John I's vow after the Battle of Aljubarrota in 1385 and became the burial church of the Aviz dynasty. Begun in 1386 by Afonso Domingues and continued by Huguet and later Mateus Fernandes, it took over a century to build and blends English-influenced Flamboyant Gothic with early Manueline work.
keyFeatures: Founder's Chapel with the tombs of John I and Philippa of Lancaster
Octagonal Unfinished Chapels, open to the sky
Square chapter house with an unsupported vault
funFacts: It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983.
An equestrian statue of the general Nuno Álvares Pereira stands in the square in front.

name: Mosteiro dos Jerónimos
aliases: Mosteiro de Santa Maria de Belém

architects.name: Diogo de Boitaca
architects.bio: An architect and engineer of unknown origin who pioneered the Manueline style at the Monastery of Jesus in Setúbal and drew the first plans of the Jerónimos Monastery in Lisbon.

architects.name: João de Castilho
architects.bio: Born in Cantabria, Castilho became one of the premier architects in the history of Portugal, moving from the Manueline towards the Plateresque and Renaissance at the Jerónimos and the Convent of Christ.

photos.alt: Richly carved white limestone church façade with a domed tower, seen from a lawn
photos.credit: Photo: Nan Palmero · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Hall church with slender carved columns spreading into a ribbed star vault
photos.caption: The church.
photos.credit: Photo: Schwarze engel · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was paid for with a tax on the profits of trade with Africa and the East.
It stands near the spot where a famous navigator set off for India in 1497.
That navigator and the poet who celebrated his voyage are both buried in its church.

summary.description: Begun on 6 January 1501 near the launch point of Vasco da Gama's voyage to India and funded by a tax on the spice trade, the monastery took a century to complete. Diogo de Boitaca drew the plans; João de Castilho, who took over around 1517, moved its ornament towards the Plateresque. Its church's slender, richly carved columns support a single vaulted space.
keyFeatures: Hall church with very slender carved columns
Wide ribbed vault over nave and aisles
Lavish Manueline ornament of ropes, plants and armillary spheres
funFacts: Vasco da Gama and Luís de Camões were reburied in new tombs in its nave in 1880.
It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983, together with the nearby Tower of Belém.

architects.name: Francisco de Arruda
architects.bio: Architect and sculptor, younger brother of Diogo de Arruda; together they assimilated Flamboyant Gothic and developed the Manueline style. He was named master of the works of the Belém stronghold.

photos.alt: Ornate white limestone fortress tower with a bastion, standing in a river
photos.credit: Photo: Nan Palmero · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Vaulted stone casemate with arches and old cannons
photos.caption: The bastion's vaulted gun hall.
photos.credit: Photo: Rodrigo Tetsuo Argenton · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built as a fortress on a rock in a river to guard a capital's harbour.
Among its carvings is one of the first European depictions of a rhinoceros.
It was finished in 1519, two years before the death of the king who ordered it.

summary.description: Built on a basalt outcrop in the Tagus to defend the entrance to Lisbon's harbour, the tower was finished in 1519 to a design by Francisco de Arruda. Its four-storey tower and hexagonal bastion are carved with Manueline ornament, Moorish-inspired turrets and the cross of the Order of Christ, and it became a ceremonial gateway for returning fleets.
keyFeatures: Loggia and balconies facing the river
funFacts: It was never in the middle of the river: it was built on a small island near the shore.
It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983, with the Jerónimos Monastery.

name: Convento de Cristo
aliases: Castle and Convent of the Order of Christ

architects.name: Diogo de Arruda
architects.bio: Portuguese architect, brother of Francisco de Arruda, who rebuilt the convent's nave for King Manuel I and designed its famous chapter-house window.

architects.name: João de Castilho
architects.bio: Born in Cantabria, Castilho became one of the premier architects in the history of Portugal, moving from the Manueline towards the Plateresque and Renaissance at the Jerónimos and the Convent of Christ.

photos.alt: Carved stone wall with a great window framed by ropes, corals and foliage, under a round window
photos.caption: The chapter-house window.

photos.caption: The Charola, the Templar round church.
photos.credit: Photo: Vitor Oliveira · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It began as a 12th-century stronghold of the Knights Templar.
Its round church was modelled on the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem.
Its most famous window is carved with ropes, corals and the emblems of a king.

summary.description: Founded as a Templar castle in the 12th century, the convent passed to the Order of Christ, which backed Portugal's voyages of discovery. From 1510 King Manuel I had Diogo de Arruda and João de Castilho rebuild the nave beside the Templar round church in the new Manueline style; its chapter-house window, carved with ropes, corals and royal emblems, is the most famous Manueline window of all.
keyFeatures: Manueline nave with the chapter-house window
Castle walls of the Templar stronghold
funFacts: A human figure at the bottom of the window probably represents its designer, Diogo de Arruda.
It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983.

architects.name: Diogo de Boitaca
architects.bio: An architect and engineer of unknown origin who pioneered the Manueline style at the Monastery of Jesus in Setúbal and drew the first plans of the Jerónimos Monastery in Lisbon.

drawings.label: View of the church and convent (18th century)

photos.caption: The nave.
photos.credit: Photo: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It is one of the first buildings in its country's late-Gothic style of the age of discovery.
Its nave is held up by twisted columns made of three intertwined shafts.
It was founded around 1490 by a noblewoman of the royal court, for a community of nuns.

summary.description: Founded around 1490 by Justa Rodrigues Pereira and sponsored by King John II, the convent church was built by Diogo de Boitaca and is the earliest known building to use Manueline decoration. Its narrow hall nave rests on spiralling columns of three twisted shafts, a motif later repeated across Portugal.
keyFeatures: Twisted columns of three intertwined shafts
Hall nave with aisles of equal height
Buttresses with gargoyles and twisted pinnacles
funFacts: Its hall-church plan prefigures the nave of the Jerónimos Monastery.
The nuns of the Order of Poor Clares were already living there in 1496.

architects.name: Afonso Álvares
architects.bio: Royal architect and military engineer who supervised the building of São Roque from 1566 to 1575; uncle of Baltasar Álvares.

architects.name: Filippo Terzi
architects.bio: Bologna-born royal architect to Philip II of Spain (Philip I of Portugal), who completed São Roque, modifying its façade, roof, ceiling and interior finishings.

photos.alt: Plain classical church front with a triangular pediment and a round window
photos.credit: Photo: Chabe01 · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Wide single nave under a painted ceiling, leading to a gilded altar
photos.caption: The nave.
photos.credit: Photo: Sergio Calleja · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was the earliest church of the Jesuits in its country's world.
Behind a plain façade lies a wide single nave designed for preaching.
One of its chapels was built in Rome from precious stones, then shipped and reassembled.

summary.description: Given to the Jesuits in 1553, São Roque was redesigned in 1565 as the first Jesuit 'auditorium church', a single wide nave for preaching, with royal architect Afonso Álvares supervising the works up to the cornice and Filippo Terzi completing them. It survived the 1755 earthquake almost unscathed, along with its painted wooden ceiling, and passed to the Lisbon Holy House of Mercy.
keyFeatures: Chapel of St John the Baptist, made in Rome
funFacts: The Chapel of St John the Baptist, by Nicola Salvi and Luigi Vanvitelli, was reportedly the most expensive chapel in Europe.
Its ceiling survived the 1755 earthquake thanks to flexible beams.

name: Mosteiro de São Vicente de Fora
aliases: Monastery of São Vicente de Fora
Igreja de São Vicente de Fora

architects.name: Filippo Terzi
architects.bio: Bologna-born military and civil engineer who came to Lisbon in 1577, was captured at Alcácer Quibir, and spent the rest of his career in Portugal.

architects.name: Juan de Herrera
architects.bio: Architect of El Escorial and the leading Spanish architect of his time; the church is thought to follow his design.

photos.alt: Tall white church façade with two towers and three arched entrances

photos.caption: The crossing.
photos.credit: Photo: T meltzer · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was rebuilt by order of a Spanish king who had also become king of this country in 1580.
Its sober twin-towered façade is a key work of Mannerism in its country.
Its former refectory became the pantheon of a royal dynasty.

summary.description: Rebuilt after Philip II of Spain became King of Portugal in 1580, the church went up between 1582 and 1629, built by Filippo Terzi to a design attributed to Juan de Herrera. Its severe twin-towered façade and vast vaulted interior made it one of the most important Mannerist buildings in Portugal; its cloisters are lined with azulejos.
keyFeatures: Barrel-vaulted nave and dome over the crossing
Royal pantheon of the Braganza dynasty
funFacts: King Ferdinand II turned the monks' refectory into a pantheon for the House of Braganza.
After 1834 the monastery became the palace of the archbishops of Lisbon.

architects.name: Baltasar Álvares
architects.bio: Jesuit-trained architect, official architect of the Jesuits in Portugal, who learned Roman Mannerism from his uncle Afonso Álvares.

photos.alt: Pale stone church façade with statues in niches, a curved Baroque top and bell towers behind
photos.credit: Photo: Alvesgaspar · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Bright barrel-vaulted nave leading to a gilded altarpiece under a dome
photos.caption: The nave.
photos.credit: Photo: Joseolgon · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built as the church of a Jesuit university college.
After the Jesuits were expelled, it became its city's cathedral in 1772.
Its façade is Mannerist below and Baroque at the top.

summary.description: Begun in 1598 to a design by Baltasar Álvares as the church of the Jesuit college of Coimbra, the building was taken over as the city's cathedral in 1772, after the Marquis of Pombal expelled the Jesuits. Its façade joins a rigid Mannerist lower part with a Baroque top, and the spacious nave ends under a dome.
keyFeatures: Façade with statues of four Jesuit saints
funFacts: The façade of the former Jesuit church of Salvador da Bahia, in Brazil, seems inspired by it.
Worship began in 1640; the church was only inaugurated in 1698.

architects.name: Nicolau Nasoni
architects.bio: Tuscan painter and architect who settled in Porto and became one of the most influential figures of Portuguese Baroque, with a theatrical style of Baroque and Rococo.

drawings.label: Entrance-level plan
drawings.alt: Plan of an elongated church with an oval nave, linked to a tower at its back
drawings.credit: Manuelvbotelho, drawing · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.credit: Photo: Bengt Nyman · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Oval nave of grey granite leading to a polychrome marble altar
photos.caption: The oval nave.
photos.credit: Photo: Scott Dexter · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built for a brotherhood of clergymen.
Its 75-metre bell tower dominates the skyline of a northern port city.
Its architect asked to be buried in its crypt.

summary.description: Built for the Brotherhood of the Clérigos by the Italian Nicolau Nasoni, the church (1732–50) was one of the first in Portugal with an elliptical nave. The tower behind it, finished in 1763 and 75.6 metres tall, became the symbol of Porto.
keyFeatures: Façade with garlands, shells and a broken pediment
funFacts: Nasoni was buried in its crypt at his own request; the exact spot is unknown.
The tower's design was inspired by Tuscan campaniles.

architects.name: João Frederico Ludovice
architects.bio: A German-born goldsmith and architect who settled in Portugal and was appointed director of the royal works at Mafra.

drawings.label: General plan
drawings.alt: Plan of a vast rectangular complex with a church at the centre of its main front and courtyards behind
drawings.credit: Ana P Rodriguez · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Very long stone façade with a twin-towered church at its centre, seen across a paved square
photos.credit: Photo: Kyle Magnuson · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Long vaulted library hall lined with gilded wooden bookcases and a chequered marble floor
photos.caption: The library.
photos.credit: Photo: Joseolgon · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It fulfilled a king's vow, made in 1711, to build a convent if the queen gave him an heir.
It was paid for largely with gold and diamonds from a colony in South America.
It combines a palace, a basilica and a friary, and its library holds about 30,000 rare books.

summary.description: King John V vowed in 1711 to build a convent if his wife gave him children; as gold and diamonds from Brazil poured in, the plan grew into a palace, basilica and friary for 330 friars. Designed by João Frederico Ludovice and built from 1717 to 1755 by up to 45,000 workers at a time, it is laid out symmetrically around the basilica at the centre of its main façade.
keyFeatures: Basilica at the centre of a symmetrical main façade
Two great towers closing the ends of the front
funFacts: Its two carillons hold 98 bells.
It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019, together with its garden and hunting park.

architects.name: João Antunes
architects.bio: Royal architect and one of the most important Baroque architects in Portugal.

photos.alt: White stone church on a Greek-cross plan with corner towers and a large dome
photos.credit: Photo: Chabe01 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Domed centre of a church with coloured marble floors and walls
photos.caption: Under the dome.
photos.credit: Photo: Kent Wang · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Its name became a national saying for a construction project that never ends.
Begun in 1682, it only received its dome and was reinaugurated in 1966.
Presidents, writers, a fado singer and a footballer are buried here.

summary.description: João Antunes designed this church on a centralised Greek-cross plan, an idea never before attempted in Portugal. Works ran from 1682 until his death in 1712, then stalled for centuries, so that 'obras de Santa Engrácia' became a byword for endless works. Converted into the National Pantheon in 1916, it finally received its dome and was reinaugurated in 1966.
keyFeatures: Large central dome, added in the 20th century
funFacts: Fado singer Amália Rodrigues and footballer Eusébio are both entombed here.
Writers Almeida Garrett and Eça de Queiroz also lie here.

name: Bom Jesus do Monte
aliases: Sanctuary of Bom Jesus do Monte
Santuário do Bom Jesus do Monte

architects.name: Carlos Amarante
aliases: Carlos Luís Ferreira da Cruz Amarante
architects.bio: A largely self-taught military engineer and architect who played a key role in the transition from Baroque and Rococo to Neoclassicism in Portugal.

photos.alt: Zigzag granite staircase with statues and fountains climbing a wooded hill to a twin-towered church
photos.credit: Photo: Glória Moura Gonçalves · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Nave of a church with a stone barrel vault leading to a gilded high altar
photos.caption: The church.
photos.credit: Photo: José Luis Filpo Cabana · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It is a hilltop pilgrimage site, reached traditionally on foot or even on the knees.
Its zigzag stairways are dedicated to the five senses and the three theological virtues.
Since 1882 a water-powered funicular, the first in the Iberian Peninsula, has carried visitors up the hill.

summary.description: The present sanctuary was begun in 1722 under Archbishop Rodrigo de Moura Telles. Its monumental stairway of 583 steps leads pilgrims past scenes of the Passion and fountains of the Five Senses and the Three Virtues, contrasting the material world with the spirit. At the top, Carlos Amarante's church (1784–1834) was one of the first Neoclassical churches in Portugal.
keyFeatures: Stairs of the Five Senses and of the Three Virtues, each with fountains
Chapels with scenes of the Passion
funFacts: Its 1882 funicular is counterbalanced by water and is still in use.
It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019.

architects.name: Mateus Vicente de Oliveira
architects.bio: Trained under Ludovice and Robillon on the building site at Mafra, he worked chiefly in the late Baroque and Rococo styles and is best remembered for the Palace of Queluz.

architects.name: Jean-Baptiste Robillon
architects.bio: French artist who had taught Oliveira at Mafra; at Queluz he was in charge of the gardens, many buildings, the Rococo interiors and the western wing that bears his name.

photos.alt: Pink and white Rococo palace front with a pediment and tall windows, seen along a formal garden
photos.credit: Photo: Kent Wang · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Mirrored, gilded throne hall with crystal chandeliers and a painted ceiling
photos.caption: The Throne Room.
photos.credit: Photo: Kent Wang · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built as a summer retreat for a king's brother, who later married his own niece, the queen.
Despite being far smaller, it is often called its country's 'Versailles'.
One of its wings is used today as the official guest house for visiting heads of state.

summary.description: Begun in 1747 by Mateus Vicente de Oliveira as a summer retreat for Peter of Braganza, later King Peter III, Queluz is one of the last great Rococo buildings in Europe. Work was interrupted by the 1755 earthquake. Oliveira's former tutor Jean-Baptiste Robillon designed the gardens, the Rococo interiors and the great western wing.
keyFeatures: Gilded throne room with mirrors and chandeliers
Formal gardens with statues and fountains
funFacts: It has been described as looking like 'a very expensive birthday cake'.
Queen Maria I lived there in seclusion after she became mentally ill.

name: Basílica da Estrela
aliases: Royal Basilica and Convent of the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus

architects.name: Mateus Vicente de Oliveira
architects.bio: Trained under Ludovice and Robillon on the building site at Mafra, he worked chiefly in the late Baroque and Rococo styles and is best remembered for the Palace of Queluz.

architects.name: Reinaldo Manuel dos Santos
architects.bio: Architect and military engineer, an apprentice on the Mafra site and one of the leading figures of Pombaline architecture and town planning after the 1755 earthquake.

photos.alt: White church front with two bell towers and statues, seen from the street
photos.credit: Photo: Alvesgaspar · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Upward view into a crossing of coloured marble vaults beneath a dome
photos.caption: The vaults and dome.
photos.credit: Photo: T meltzer · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: A princess vowed to build it if she bore an heir; she could only fulfil the vow after becoming queen.
It was the first church in the world dedicated to the Sacred Heart of Jesus.
Its foundress is buried in its right transept.

summary.description: Ordered by Queen Maria I to fulfil a vow for an heir, the basilica was begun in 1779 by Mateus Vicente de Oliveira and continued after his death by Reinaldo Manuel dos Santos. It was the first church in the world dedicated to the Sacred Heart of Jesus and the most important architectural work of her reign.
keyFeatures: Twin bell towers flanking the front
funFacts: It houses a nativity scene by Joaquim Machado de Castro with more than 500 cork and terracotta figures.

architects.name: José da Costa e Silva
architects.bio: Trained in Rome, he became royal architect and helped establish Neoclassical architecture in Portugal and colonial Brazil.

architects.name: Francisco Xavier Fabri
architects.bio: Architect from Medicina, near Bologna, who settled in Portugal and took charge of the Ajuda project after the royal family fled to Brazil.

drawings.alt: Plan of a huge palace around a large courtyard, with the executed part shown in solid black
drawings.credit: Published in the journal of the Associação dos Architectos Civis Portuguezes · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

photos.credit: Photo: Unknown photographer, Library of Congress · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Red-carpeted stone staircase rising between carved white walls
photos.caption: A staircase.
photos.credit: Photo: Pedro J Pacheco · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It stands on the site of a wooden royal residence built after the 1755 earthquake.
Works slowed to a crawl when the royal family fled to Brazil in 1807.
Its unfinished west side was only completed in the 21st century, to house the crown jewels.

summary.description: Begun in 1796 on the site of the wooden 'Real Barraca', the palace was redesigned in the Neoclassical style by José da Costa e Silva and Francisco Xavier Fabri. After the court fled Napoleon's troops to Brazil in 1807 the works dragged on, and only part of the vast plan was built. It became a permanent royal residence under King Luís I and Queen Maria Pia.
keyFeatures: Long Neoclassical façades with corner pavilions
Interiors designed for Queen Maria Pia
Plan far larger than what was built
New west wing for the Royal Treasure Museum
funFacts: Since 2022 it has housed the Royal Treasure Museum with the Portuguese crown jewels.
Possidónio da Silva turned one of its side façades into the main one.

architects.name: José da Costa e Silva
architects.bio: Trained in Rome, he became royal architect and helped establish Neoclassical architecture in Portugal and colonial Brazil.

photos.alt: Yellow and white theatre front with a clock, balcony and three entrance arches on a paved square
photos.credit: Photo: Lrocha · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Horseshoe auditorium with tiers of gilded boxes and a crowned royal box
photos.caption: The auditorium.
photos.credit: Photo: Nonducorduco1971 · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It replaced an opera house destroyed in the 1755 earthquake.
It was built in only six months and opened in 1793.
Its design draws on great opera houses in Naples and Milan.

summary.description: Opened by Queen Maria I on 30 June 1793 to replace the Tejo Opera House lost in the 1755 earthquake, the theatre was built in only six months to a design by José da Costa e Silva. Its interior is inspired by the San Carlo in Naples and La Scala in Milan, and its façade by La Scala.
keyFeatures: Horseshoe auditorium with tiers of boxes
funFacts: It was named for Princess Charlotte (Carlota) of Spain, wife of the future King John VI.
The first opera staged there was Cimarosa's 'La ballerina amante'.

architects.name: John Carr
architects.bio: Considered in his day the leading architect in the north of England, he worked mostly in the Palladian style, notably at Harewood House and Buxton Crescent.

photos.alt: Long granite Neoclassical building with a columned central pavilion topped by statues
photos.credit: Photo: Rodrigo Tetsuo Argenton · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Old pharmacy with carved wooden cabinets full of glass jars under a vaulted ceiling
photos.caption: The old pharmacy, now a museum.
photos.credit: Photo: Rodrigo Tetsuo Argenton · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Its architect was English, best known for country houses in the Palladian style.
It was begun in 1770 on open land at the edge of its city.
Only about two-thirds of the original plan was ever built.

summary.description: Begun on 15 July 1770 on what was then the edge of Porto, the hospital was designed by the English architect John Carr and is described as the most Palladian building in Portugal. It was inaugurated in 1824 with only about two-thirds of the project executed, and it is still a working hospital.
keyFeatures: Historic pharmacy, now part of the hospital museum
funFacts: Its architect's best-known work is Harewood House in Yorkshire.

architects.name: Wilhelm Ludwig von Eschwege
architects.bio: A geologist, mineralogist and mining engineer who served the Portuguese court in Portugal and Brazil, and worked as an amateur architect.

photos.alt: Yellow, red and grey castle-palace with domes and towers on a forested hilltop
photos.credit: Photo: Chabe01 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Round room with a central column spreading into a palm-like vault, hung with antlers
photos.caption: The Stag Room.
photos.credit: Photo: Dale Cruse · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built over the ruins of a monastery wrecked by lightning and then by the 1755 earthquake.
A king consort born in Germany commissioned it as a summer residence for the royal family.
It is one of the major expressions of 19th-century Romanticism and one of the Seven Wonders of Portugal.

summary.description: King consort Ferdinand II bought the ruined Hieronymite monastery on a Sintra hilltop in 1838 and had Baron von Eschwege rebuild it as a Romantic summer palace between 1842 and 1854. The king and Queen Maria II intervened decisively in its decoration and symbolism.
keyFeatures: Brightly coloured towers, domes and battlements
Stag Room with a palm-like central vault
Built over the remains of a Hieronymite monastery
funFacts: It later passed to Ferdinand's second wife, Elisa Hensler, Countess of Edla.
It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

architects.name: Luigi Manini
architects.bio: Born in Crema, he came to Lisbon in 1879 as a scenographer for the São Carlos opera house and went on to design Neo-Manueline fantasies such as the Quinta da Regaleira in Sintra.

photos.alt: Ornate stone palace with a tall pinnacled tower and carved arcades, seen across a formal garden
photos.credit: Photo: Vitor Oliveira · CC BY 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Old photograph of a grand hall with a carved fireplace, arches and painted walls
photos.caption: A hall, c. 1923.
photos.credit: Photo: Unknown photographer, postcard c. 1923 · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was planned as a royal residence for a queen but became a hotel instead.
It stands in a forest garden created by monks next to their former convent.
It imitates the 16th-century style of Jerónimos and the Tower of Belém.

summary.description: Built between 1888 and 1907 beside a former convent in the Buçaco forest, the palace was first meant as a residence for Queen Maria Pia before becoming a hotel. Luigi Manini designed it as a Romantic, Neo-Manueline evocation of the Age of Discovery, and was succeeded by Nicola Bigaglia, José Alexandre Soares and Manuel Joaquim Norte Júnior.
keyFeatures: Azulejo panels by Jorge Colaço on the Discoveries
Interiors with stucco imitating Manueline rib vaults
funFacts: It was completed shortly before the fall of the Portuguese monarchy in 1910.
It has been a National Monument since 2018.

architects.name: Joaquim da Costa Lima Júnior
architects.bio: Porto architect who led the project from 1840 to 1860 and gave it its general Neo-Palladian design.

architects.name: Gustavo Adolfo Gonçalves e Sousa
architects.bio: Architect who later designed the palace's grand stairway and its Arab Room.

photos.alt: Large Neoclassical palace with a pedimented front, seen among the roofs of a hillside city by a river
photos.credit: Photo: Alvesgaspar · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Octagonal hall covered in gilded Moorish-style stucco arabesques, with horseshoe arches and a patterned ceiling
photos.caption: The Arab Room.
photos.credit: Photo: Nan Palmero · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built by the merchants of its city as the seat of their commercial association.
It stands on the ruins of a convent's cloisters, burned during the Liberal Wars in 1832.
Its most famous room imitates the Alhambra, although the rest of the building is Neoclassical.

summary.description: After Queen Maria II gave the ruins of the São Francisco convent to Porto's merchants in 1841, the Commercial Association built its seat there to plans by Joaquim da Costa Lima Júnior, a Neoclassical palace of Palladian influence. The structure was finished by about 1850, but the lavish interiors took until 1910; Gustavo Adolfo Gonçalves e Sousa added the stairway and the Arab Room.
keyFeatures: Courtyard covered by a metal and glass dome by Tomás Soler
funFacts: It has been a National Monument since 1982.
It stands right beside the church of São Francisco, the surviving part of the old convent.

architects.name: Luigi Manini
architects.bio: Born in Crema, he came to Lisbon in 1879 as a scenographer for the São Carlos opera house and went on to design Neo-Manueline fantasies such as the Buçaco Palace.

photos.alt: Lacy grey stone mansion with pinnacles and a turret, rising above a garden
photos.credit: Photo: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Room panelled in carved dark wood with a painted frieze above a monumental doorway
photos.caption: A panelled room.
photos.credit: Photo: Jorge Lobo · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Its owner, nicknamed 'the Millionaire', bought the estate in 1892.
Its park hides grottoes, tunnels and two 'initiation wells' that were never meant to hold water.
Its symbols allude to alchemy, Freemasonry, the Knights Templar and the Rosicrucians.

summary.description: António Augusto Carvalho Monteiro bought the estate in 1892 and, with Luigi Manini, built a Romantic palace, chapel and park between 1904 and 1910. Manini's architecture evokes Roman, Gothic, Renaissance and Manueline styles, and the park is filled with buildings and passages charged with esoteric symbolism.
keyFeatures: Neo-Manueline palace with pinnacles and a turret
Initiation Well with a 27-metre spiral staircase
Grottoes, lakes and tunnels in the park
funFacts: The Initiation Well's nine flights of stairs may allude to the nine founders of the Knights Templar.
Before Carvalho Monteiro, it belonged to the Viscountess of Regaleira.

architects.name: José Marques da Silva
architects.bio: Trained at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris under Victor Laloux, he combined the Beaux-Arts tradition with practical modern planning and long directed the Porto School of Fine Arts.

photos.alt: Granite Beaux-Arts building with a clock in a curved pediment and a mansard roof, on a street corner
photos.credit: Photo: Andrey Filippov 安德烈 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Entrance hall lined with large blue-and-white tile panels under tall arched windows and a clock
photos.caption: The vestibule.
photos.credit: Photo: Michael Gaylard · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It stands on the site of a Benedictine convent founded by King Manuel I in 1518.
Its vestibule is lined with about 20,000 painted tiles showing scenes of the nation's history.
Trains reach it through a tunnel carved into the hill behind it.

summary.description: Built on the site of the Benedictine convent of São Bento da Avé Maria, Porto's central station was designed by José Marques da Silva in the French Beaux-Arts manner. Works began in 1904, and the definitive building opened on 5 October 1916. Its vestibule holds about 20,000 azulejo tiles by Jorge Colaço.
keyFeatures: U-shaped plan facing the Praça Almeida Garrett
Central atrium flanked by two volumes
Azulejo panels by Jorge Colaço, about 551 m²
funFacts: A provisional station had opened on the site in 1896.
The city removed Marques da Silva from the project in 1909.

architects.name: José Luís Monteiro
architects.bio: One of the most influential Portuguese architects of the late 19th century, and teacher of Porfírio Pardal Monteiro at the Lisbon School of Fine Arts.

photos.alt: Ornate white stone façade with a clock turret, pinnacles and rows of carved arched windows
photos.credit: Photo: Harvey Barrison · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Concourse with an iron roof truss, skylights and pointed arched openings
photos.caption: The concourse.
photos.credit: Photo: Chabe01 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was originally called 'Central Station', a name still carved on its façade.
Trains reach it through a tunnel almost 3 km long under the city.
Its entrance has two intertwined horseshoe-shaped portals.

summary.description: Commissioned by the Portuguese Royal Railway Company and designed in 1886–87 by José Luís Monteiro, the station was completed in 1890 at the end of a tunnel of over 2.9 km. Its Neo-Manueline façade is a Romantic recreation of the exuberant style of early 16th-century Portugal.
funFacts: The station was closed to trains from 2004 to 2008 while the tunnel was renewed.

architects.name: Francisco Xavier Esteves
architects.bio: Engineer, professor and politician, considered the man who introduced reinforced concrete to civil construction in Portugal.

photos.alt: Narrow shopfront with a Gothic-style gable, painted figures and tall windows

photos.alt: Forked wooden staircase rising to a gallery under a stained-glass ceiling, between walls of books
photos.caption: The staircase.
photos.credit: Photo: Nan Palmero · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It is a shop, founded by a Frenchman in 1869 and later run by two brothers.
Its present building opened in 1906.
Inside, a forked staircase climbs to a gallery under a large stained-glass window with the motto 'Decus in Labore'.

summary.description: The bookshop founded by Ernesto Chardron passed to the brothers José and António Lello, who hired engineer Francisco Xavier Esteves to build new premises on Rua das Carmelitas, inaugurated in 1906. The façade mixes Neo-Gothic and Art Nouveau; inside, a forked staircase rises to a gallery beneath an 8-by-3.5-metre stained-glass window.
keyFeatures: Neo-Gothic gable with painted figures of Art and Science
Forked staircase to a first-floor gallery
Large stained-glass skylight with the owners' monogram
funFacts: It was called Livraria Chardron until 1919.

architects.name: José Marques da Silva
architects.bio: Trained at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris under Victor Laloux, he combined the Beaux-Arts tradition with practical modern planning and long directed the Porto School of Fine Arts.

photos.alt: Large stone theatre with Ionic columns, arched windows and sculpted reliefs, on a square
photos.credit: Photo: Vitor Oliveira · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Foyer with marbled red columns, gilded capitals and a coffered ceiling hung with lamps
photos.caption: The foyer.
photos.credit: Photo: Joseolgon · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It replaced an 18th-century royal theatre destroyed by fire in 1908.
Its architect won the competition for the new building and work began in 1911.
It opened in 1920 with a performance of Verdi's 'Aida'.

summary.description: The original Royal Theatre of São João, opened in 1798, burned down on 11 April 1908. José Marques da Silva won the competition for a new theatre on the same site, and building began in 1911. It was complete in 1918 and inaugurated on 7 March 1920 with Verdi's 'Aida'.
keyFeatures: Reliefs of Kindness, Pain, Hatred and Love by Diogo de Macedo and Sousa Caldas
Horseshoe-shaped auditorium with a painted ceiling
funFacts: From 1932 it also worked as a cinema, the São João Cine.

architects.name: Raul Lino
architects.bio: Architect, designer and theorist of the 'Casa Portuguesa', an idealised concept of Portuguese residential architecture; many of his houses stand in Cascais and Sintra.

photos.alt: White country house with a long arcaded upper gallery and tiled roofs, beside an open yard

photos.alt: Grand staircase with carved wooden balustrade and statues, against a blue-and-white tile panel
photos.caption: The grand staircase.
photos.credit: Photo: Senhormario · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built for a republican politician who proclaimed the Republic from a city hall balcony in 1910.
Its owner left it to his town in his will, asking that it be kept as a museum.
Its architect was the leading theorist of the 'Portuguese house'.

summary.description: Raul Lino designed this house, built between 1905 and 1909, for José Relvas, the republican who proclaimed the Republic in Lisbon on 5 October 1910 and later briefly led the government. Relvas left it and its collections to the municipality of Alpiarça, and it opened as a museum on 15 May 1960.
keyFeatures: White walls and tiled roofs inspired by traditional Portuguese houses
Rooms kept with the owner's art collections
funFacts: José Relvas died in the house in 1929.

architects.name: Charles Siclis
architects.bio: Parisian architect and decorator, author of various projects for Paris theatres.

architects.name: José Marques da Silva
architects.bio: Trained at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris under Victor Laloux, he combined the Beaux-Arts tradition with practical modern planning and long directed the Porto School of Fine Arts.

photos.alt: Pink Art Deco villa with a rounded bay, vertical window strips and a terrace of steps
photos.credit: Photo: Francisco Anzola · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Doorway with a gilded wrought-iron grille between pale columns, opening onto a sequence of rooms
photos.caption: The salon door.
photos.credit: Photo: Daniel VILLAFRUELA. · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was commissioned by an aristocrat of the textile industry who inherited the estate in 1923.
A French architect drew the project; a Portuguese architect carried it out and kept changing it.
It stands in a park whose grounds now also hold a contemporary art museum.

summary.description: The 2nd Count of Vizela had the house designed by the French architect Charles Siclis; its execution fell to José Marques da Silva, whose successive changes delayed the works until 1940. Considered a unique example of Art Deco in Portugal, it was bought by the State in 1986 and became the core of the Serralves Foundation.
keyFeatures: Gardens by Jacques Gréber, designed in 1932
funFacts: The Count moved in only in 1944 and sold it about ten years later.
The Serralves buildings were classified as a National Monument in 2012.

architects.name: Cassiano Branco
architects.bio: One of the most important Portuguese architects of the first half of the 20th century, also known for the Hotel Vitória and the Portugal dos Pequenitos park.

photos.alt: Cream building with horizontal bands of windows, round porthole openings and a dark stone base
photos.credit: Photo: Joehawkins · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Auditorium with tiers of boxes, a gilded relief above the stage and a ceiling ring lit in blue
photos.caption: The auditorium.
photos.credit: Photo: Joseolgon · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It replaced a garden-hall that had been the meeting place of its city's society.
It opened in December 1941 and is one of its city's main concert venues.
In 1995 its sale to a Brazilian church caused a popular revolt, and the city council bought it instead.

summary.description: Built on the site of the Passos Manuel garden-hall, the Coliseu was designed by Cassiano Branco with Júlio de Brito, with the Parisian theatre architect Charles Siclis also invited onto the project. It opened on 19 December 1941 and is an example of Streamline Moderne and Art Deco in Porto.
keyFeatures: Horizontal bands of windows and porthole openings
Large auditorium with tiers of boxes
Ceiling lit from a central ring
funFacts: After the protests of 1995 the city council bought it in 1996.
A fire in 1996 destroyed the stage and main hall; it reopened on 17 December that year.

name: Igreja de Nossa Senhora de Fátima
aliases: Church of Our Lady of Fátima
Igreja de Nossa Senhora do Rosário de Fátima
Our Lady of the Rosary of Fátima

architects.name: Porfírio Pardal Monteiro
architects.bio: One of the most important Portuguese architects of the first half of the 20th century, student of José Luís Monteiro and author of the Instituto Superior Técnico campus in Lisbon.

photos.alt: White stone church with a tall slender bell tower ending in a pointed spire, on a street corner
