photos.alt: Nave with pointed concrete arches leading to an apse filled with blue stained glass
photos.caption: The nave.
photos.credit: Photo: Palickap · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was commissioned in 1933 and consecrated in October 1938.
It won the Valmor Prize for architecture in the year it was consecrated.
It is considered a landmark of its country's Modernism, with a flat roof and an asymmetrical composition.

summary.description: Commissioned from Porfírio Pardal Monteiro in 1933, the church was consecrated in October 1938 and won that year's Valmor Prize. It keeps Art Deco traits in its fragmented, ornamented volumes, but its modernity lies in its asymmetry, flat roof and the expression of its structure. Its nave is lit by tall stained-glass windows between great concrete arches.
keyFeatures: Circular baptistery with a stepped concrete dome
Great concrete arches carrying the nave roof
Apse walls filled with stained glass
funFacts: Raul Rodrigues Lima and João Faria da Costa worked on the project in Pardal Monteiro's studio.

architects.name: Porfírio Pardal Monteiro
architects.bio: One of the most important Portuguese architects of the first half of the 20th century, a student of José Luís Monteiro and a teacher at the Instituto Superior Técnico.

architects.name: Luís Benavente
architects.bio: Lisbon architect who collaborated with Pardal Monteiro on the Alameda campus.

photos.alt: Long cream-rendered building with rows of tall green-framed windows divided by vertical ribs
photos.credit: Photo: João Carvalho · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Stone stair with a curved metal handrail turning beneath a skylight
photos.caption: A stairwell.
photos.credit: Photo: Garsd · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It belongs to Portugal's engineering school, founded in 1911, and was the first academic institution in the country to have its own campus.
Its director in 1927 launched the project, and construction ran from 1928 to 1935.
Seven buildings are laid out on a grid, alternating with formal gardens.

summary.description: In 1927 the school's director Duarte Pacheco started the project for a new campus and commissioned Porfírio Pardal Monteiro, who worked with the architect Luís Benavente. Built from 1928 to 1935 and inaugurated the next year, it was the first Portuguese academic institution with its own campus. Its sober Art Deco-tinged modernism gets its grandeur from the volumes of the buildings rather than from decoration.
keyFeatures: Seven buildings arranged on a grid
Sober, restrained decoration of its era
Grandeur achieved through volumes, not ornament
funFacts: A statue of a woman holding a square and compass by Salvador Barata Feyo, made for a 1948 exhibition, now stands on the campus.
The Civil Engineering and Architecture Pavilion and the North and South towers were added in the 1950s.

architects.name: Porfírio Pardal Monteiro
architects.bio: One of the most important Portuguese architects of the first half of the 20th century, a student of José Luís Monteiro and a teacher at the Instituto Superior Técnico.

photos.alt: Broad low building with a recessed central entrance and pink-red panels between ranks of windows, seen across a lawn
photos.credit: Photo: Ilham Mufti Laksono · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Large reading room under a timber coffered ceiling, with tall windows and a tapestry on the end wall
photos.caption: The reading room.
photos.credit: Photo: pru_mitchell · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built because the library's historic home, a convent, had become too small for its collections.
Work began in 1958, and the books were moved in 1969.
It stands on the west side of a city park, Campo Grande.

summary.description: The National Library outgrew its home in the Convento de São Francisco, so a purpose-designed building was planned. Work began in 1958 to a design by Porfírio Pardal Monteiro, and the collections were transferred to the new building in the Campo Grande area in 1969. It was very modern for its time.
keyFeatures: Purpose-designed home for the national collections
Tower of deposits for book storage
Designed by Pardal Monteiro, very modern for its time
Site on the west side of the Campo Grande garden
funFacts: The storage tower was enlarged between 2008 and 2011, adding 6,300 m².
Its reading service for visually impaired readers has produced Braille and audio books since 1969.

architects.name: Ruy Jervis d'Athouguia
architects.bio: Lisbon architect, one of the three members of the team that won the competition for the Gulbenkian Foundation headquarters.

architects.name: Pedro Cid
architects.bio: Architect of the third generation of Portuguese modernists, who helped change mentalities in post-war architecture.

architects.name: Alberto Pessoa
architects.bio: Architect and member of the team that won the competition for the Gulbenkian Foundation buildings.

photos.alt: Long raised concrete building with planted terraces, overlooking a lawn dotted with café parasols
photos.credit: Photo: Kilian Evang · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Timber-ceilinged room with a floor-to-ceiling window onto a garden, set with two red chairs
photos.caption: A room facing the garden.
photos.credit: Photo: Jules Verne Times Two · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: The site was part of a park bought in 1957, and the buildings were designed by a team that won a competition.
The landscape architects of its garden included Gonçalo Ribeiro Telles.
It was designed as a showcase for a single collector's collection, rather than adapted from an older building.

summary.description: A competition for the foundation's buildings and park was won by a team including Alberto Pessoa, Pedro Cid and Ruy Jervis d'Athouguia, with the landscape architects António Viana Barreto and Gonçalo Ribeiro Telles designing the surrounding park. The buildings and gardens were inaugurated on 2 October 1969, and the complex won the Valmor Prize in 1975.
keyFeatures: Park by Viana Barreto and Ribeiro Telles
Museum designed as a showcase for its collection
funFacts: The Centro de Arte Moderna opened in 1983 as Portugal's first museum of modern art.
A sculpture panel by Artur Rosa was installed in the headquarters in 1962.

name: Igreja do Sagrado Coração de Jesus
aliases: Church of the Sacred Heart of Jesus

architects.name: Nuno Portas
architects.bio: Architect born in Vila Viçosa who worked with Nuno Teotónio Pereira on this church.

architects.name: Nuno Teotónio Pereira
architects.bio: Lisbon architect trained at the Lisbon School of Fine Arts and the author of several Valmor Prize buildings.

photos.alt: Rough concrete stairway rising beside a stark modern building with a tall blue glass strip, framed by trees
photos.credit: Photo: Felipe Tofani · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Nave of textured brick-like walls under a concrete roof grid, lit by narrow coloured glass
photos.caption: The nave.
photos.credit: Photo: PenrodCenturion · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It won the first prize in the competition held for its design.
It was built between 1962 and 1967 and inaugurated only in 1970.
It is a landmark of exposed concrete: its panels were prefabricated on site with the stone aggregate left visible.

summary.description: Designed by Nuno Portas and Nuno Teotónio Pereira, who won the competition for it, the church was built from 1962 to 1967 and inaugurated on 25 June 1970. It was a deliberately 'experimental' work and a turning point for religious architecture, using exposed concrete and glass and playing with light. It won the Valmor Prize in 1975.
keyFeatures: Prefabricated panels of white limestone aggregate in white cement
Integration with the volumes of surrounding buildings
funFacts: The architects argued that a 'constructive lie' was unacceptable in church architecture.
The aggregate of its panels is white limestone from Vila Viçosa.

name: Bloco das Águas Livres
aliases: Edifício na Praça das Águas Livres

architects.name: Nuno Teotónio Pereira
architects.bio: Lisbon architect trained at the Lisbon School of Fine Arts and the author of several Valmor Prize buildings.

architects.name: Bartolomeu Costa Cabral
architects.bio: Lisbon architect, considered one of the leading figures in the turn of the modern movement in Portuguese architecture; he joined this project as a beginner.

photos.alt: Ten-storey pink and grey apartment block with rows of balconies above a ground-floor arcade
photos.credit: Photo: Manuelvbotelho · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Entrance hall with a pastel column, a stair and a wall of mailboxes lit by low sun
photos.caption: The entrance hall.
photos.credit: Photo: DiogoBaptista · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It is an apartment block, planned as an income-producing building in a decade of such buildings.
It was designed between 1953 and 1955 and built in 1956.
Its architect wanted to create 'a space for modern life'.

summary.description: Designed by Nuno Teotónio Pereira with Bartolomeu Costa Cabral on the Praça das Águas Livres, in Lisbon's Rato area, this housing block was drawn up between 1953 and 1955 and built in 1956. Its programme would mark the architecture of its time and later years, and aimed to create a space for modern life.
keyFeatures: Entrance hall with a wall of mailboxes
Collaboration between Teotónio Pereira and the young Costa Cabral
funFacts: The first plans were submitted for licensing on 30 August 1953, as 17 drawings and a written description.

name: Casa de Chá da Boa Nova

architects.name: Álvaro Siza Vieira
architects.bio: Porto architect and educator, a former student of Fernando Távora and winner of the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 1992.

photos.credit: Photo: Jeremy Weate · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Dark-wood staircase leading up to a lounge with a table lamp
photos.caption: The entrance stair.
photos.credit: Photo: 準建築人手札網站 Forgemind ArchiMedia · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was one of its architect's first works, passed to him by his teacher after the site was chosen.
It was remodelled in 1991 after a strong storm hit the building.
It sits among rocks on the Atlantic coast and uses wood on its floors, walls and ceilings.

summary.description: Built between 1958 and 1963 on the rocks at Boa Nova, in Leça da Palmeira, this tea house and restaurant was one of Álvaro Siza's first works. His teacher Fernando Távora chose the site and handed him the project. Access is by a stepped path set into the rocks that alternately reveals and hides the sea.
keyFeatures: Stepped pathway integrated into the rocks
Wood on floors, walls and ceilings
funFacts: After the 1991 storm, Siza supervised the renovation following his original drawings.
It is close to the tidal pools of Leça da Palmeira, designed by the same architect.

name: Pousada de Santa Marinha
aliases: Mosteiro de Santa Marinha da Costa

architects.name: Fernando Távora
architects.bio: Architect and professor who became a key figure in the modernisation of the Porto School; two of his former students, Siza and Souto de Moura, later won the Pritzker Prize.

style: Contemporary conversion of a historic monastery

photos.alt: Twin-towered Baroque church front above a stairway, seen between trees
photos.credit: Photo: Vitor Oliveira · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Arcaded cloister around a fountain and clipped box hedges
photos.caption: The cloister.
photos.credit: Photo: GFreihalter · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It is a former monastery whose site is believed to have been the palace of the early Portuguese counts.
The State bought it in 1972 and began restoration five years later.
Its architect won the National Architecture Prize in 1987 for turning it into a hotel.

summary.description: The Hieronymite monastery of Santa Marinha da Costa, on a hillside above Guimarães, was bought by the State in 1972, and its restoration began five years later. Fernando Távora designed its reconstruction and adaptation as a pousada, a work that earned him the National Architecture Prize of 1987. A new lowered block painted in a contrasting maroon contains 27 of the rooms.
keyFeatures: Historic church and monastery wings kept
New low block with spare modern rooms
Archaeological traces exposed in the walls
funFacts: The hotel's entrance is the old refectory, where the granite frame of the reading pulpit survives.
It belongs to the Pousadas de Portugal network, as a 'Historic Pousada'.

name: Museu de Serralves
aliases: Museu de Arte Contemporânea de Serralves

architects.name: Álvaro Siza Vieira
architects.bio: Porto architect and educator, a former student of Fernando Távora and winner of the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 1992.

photos.alt: White rendered boxy volumes with a recessed doorway and a single square window, on a lawn among trees
photos.credit: Photo: Gabriel de Andrade Fernandes · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Large gallery of white and brown walls with a skylight and a polished timber floor
photos.caption: A gallery.
photos.credit: Photo: Gabriel de Andrade Fernandes · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Its architect signed the contract in March 1991, one year before winning the Pritzker Prize.
It opened in June 1999 in the park of an Art Deco villa.
It is surrounded by a park where artworks stand beside native trees.

summary.description: The Serralves Foundation signed a contract with Álvaro Siza on 6 March 1991 to design a museum of contemporary art in the park of Serralves, and it was inaugurated on 6 June 1999. It has become the second most visited museum in Portugal. In 2023 a new wing by Siza opened, partly to hold part of his archive and the legacy of Manoel de Oliveira.
keyFeatures: Set in the park of the Serralves Foundation
Part of a group with the Art Deco villa and the park
Later extension, the Ala Álvaro Siza (2023)
funFacts: It stands in the same park as the Casa de Serralves, an Art Deco villa.

aliases: Faculty of Architecture of the University of Porto
Faculdade de Arquitetura da Universidade do Porto

photos.alt: Long library hall with timber tables and bookshelves under a sloping skylight
photos.caption: The library.
photos.credit: Photo: Leon · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It houses a school created in 1979, the successor of an architecture course taught at the city's fine arts school.
Construction began in 1985, on a site above a river and next to an old estate.
Its architect was a former student and later professor of the school.

summary.description: Created in 1979, the faculty got its new premises from Álvaro Siza, a former student and later professor, who first drew a renovation of the Quinta da Póvoa house and the Carlos Ramos pavilion in 1985–86. The complex opens towards the Douro in several fragmented volumes, with four towers linked by a half-buried transverse gallery. The premises were completed in 1992.
keyFeatures: Stone walls linking the building to the old estate garden
Library, museum and auditorium in a northern building
funFacts: The U-shaped Carlos Ramos pavilion was shaped by the trees and roots on the site.
The move into the new building took until 1996.

architects.name: Artur Andrade
architects.bio: Porto-born architect, one of the introducers of the Modern Movement in Portugal and a member of ODAM, the Organisation of Modern Architects.

photos.alt: Curved white corner with tall glazed windows and a carved relief panel, on a city square
photos.credit: Photo: Manuel de Sousa · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Dark stairwell rising past a wall painted with swirling shapes
photos.caption: The stairwell.
photos.credit: Photo: Acfmagalhaes · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It replaced an older cinema on the same site; the old building was demolished in 1944.
It was inaugurated on 3 June 1947, and under the dictatorship its frescoes were ordered hidden in 1948.
It reopened as a cultural venue in 2006.

summary.description: Rebuilt by the architect Artur Andrade in the Art Deco style between 1944 and 1947, the Batalha is a four-storey trapezoidal structure with overhanging upper floors. Its decoration included frescoes by Júlio Pomar and a bas-relief by Américo Braga. In 1948 censors ordered the frescoes hidden and the relief altered to remove a sickle and a hammer.
keyFeatures: Foyers in varnished woods, glass, copper and metal
Floors of black polished marmorite with brass inlay
funFacts: One of Pomar's two frescoes was still unfinished at the inauguration because the artist was in prison for opposing the regime.
It re-opened in 2006 as a cultural and concert venue.

architects.name: Álvaro Siza Vieira
architects.bio: Porto architect and educator, a former student of Fernando Távora and winner of the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 1992.

photos.alt: Thin concrete canopy sagging between two massive porticoed blocks, over an open square

photos.alt: White stairwell of sharp planes rising under a hidden skylight
photos.caption: A stairwell.
photos.credit: Photo: GualdimG · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It housed its country's national representation at a world's fair in the late 1990s.
Its entrance square is covered by a pre-stressed concrete canopy based on the idea of a sheet of paper resting on two bricks.
After standing empty for years, it was handed over to a university in 2015.

summary.description: Designed by Álvaro Siza for Expo '98, the pavilion housed Portugal's national representation at the world's fair. Its entrance square is covered by an imposing canopy of pre-stressed concrete, inspired by a sheet of paper laid on two bricks. Left empty after the exhibition, it was handed over to the University of Lisbon in 2015.
keyFeatures: Covered entrance square open to the city
Canopy inspired by a sheet of paper laid on two bricks
funFacts: In 2015 it was nearly sold to settle part of the Expo company's debt to the State.
Proposals for its reuse ranged from a seat for the Council of Ministers to an architecture museum.

architects.name: Eduardo Souto de Moura
architects.bio: Porto School architect, alongside Távora and Siza, who received the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2011 and the Wolf Prize in Arts in 2013.

photos.credit: Photo: 準建築人手札網站 Forgemind ArchiMedia · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.caption: Under the stands.
photos.credit: Photo: 準建築人手札網站 Forgemind ArchiMedia · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built as a venue for a European football championship in 2004.
Its nickname comes from having been carved into the side of a hill.
Its architect was awarded the Pritzker Prize partly for this design.

summary.description: Eduardo Souto de Moura designed the home of Sporting Clube de Braga for Euro 2004, carving it into the side of a hill, hence its nickname, The Quarry. Built from 2002 to 2003, it opened on 30 December 2003. The rock excavation pushed its cost far above the estimate, making it the most expensive of the ten new Euro 2004 stadiums.
keyFeatures: Carved into the side of a hill at its south end
Home of Sporting Clube de Braga
funFacts: Its final cost reached about €200 million, against an initial estimate of €29.9 million.
It hosted two Euro 2004 matches, including Netherlands v Latvia.

architects.name: Eduardo Souto de Moura
architects.bio: Porto School architect, alongside Távora and Siza, who received the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2011 and the Wolf Prize in Arts in 2013.

photos.alt: Red concrete museum with two tall pyramid-shaped towers, set among trees on a lawn
photos.credit: Photo: 準建築人手札網站 Forgemind ArchiMedia · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Pale gallery room with an angled ceiling and small framed works on the walls
photos.caption: A gallery.
photos.credit: Photo: Leon · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It is a museum dedicated to the work of a single woman artist, who attended its opening.
It opened in September 2009, and its building won the Secil Architecture Prize in 2010.
It is made of several bodies of red concrete surrounded by trees.

summary.description: Opened in September 2009 in the presence of the artist, this museum in Cascais is devoted to the work of Paula Rego. Eduardo Souto de Moura's building is formed of several red concrete volumes surrounded by trees, and it won the Secil Architecture Prize in 2010.
funFacts: It holds a permanent exhibition of Paula Rego's work and two temporary exhibitions a year.

architects.name: Rem Koolhaas
architects.bio: Dutch architect, theorist and urbanist, founder of OMA, often cited as a representative of deconstructivism and author of 'Delirious New York'.

photos.alt: Faceted white concrete block like a cut gem, with a large window and a stair to its entrance, on a paved plaza
photos.credit: Photo: Joseolgon · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Shoebox hall with gold-patterned wood walls and a wall of glass at the end
photos.caption: The main hall.
photos.credit: Photo: Dion Hinchcliffe · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was planned to mark the year its city was European Capital of Culture, 2001, but opened four years late.
It stands on the site of an old tram terminus at a large roundabout.
It was the first building in its country designed from the start to be dedicated exclusively to music.

summary.description: Commissioned for Porto's year as European Capital of Culture in 2001, the concert house was won in an international competition by Rem Koolhaas and OMA in 1999 and built on the old tram terminus at the Boavista roundabout. It was inaugurated on 15 April 2005. The building is a nine-storey asymmetrical polyhedron clad in white concrete, cut by large glass windows.
funFacts: The New York Times critic Nicolai Ouroussoff called it the most attractive project Koolhaas had ever built.
Lou Reed played on the day it opened to the public.

architects.name: Santiago Calatrava
architects.bio: Architect, structural engineer, sculptor and painter known for bridges with leaning pylons and stations, stadiums and museums whose forms resemble living organisms.

photos.alt: Station entrance under a fan of white steel ribs and glass, glowing at dusk above a road
photos.credit: Photo: Kent Wang · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Platforms under a forest of white steel 'trees' branching into a glass roof, with a red train
photos.caption: The platforms.
photos.credit: Photo: Kent Wang · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It opened in May 1998 as part of the celebrations for a world's fair.
It was considered the largest intermodal station in its country when it opened.
Its designer, also a structural engineer, is known for works whose forms resemble living organisms.

summary.description: Designed by Santiago Calatrava in 1995 and inaugurated on 19 May 1998 for Expo '98, the station was designed to provide multiple connections between zones of the Lisbon metropolitan area. It won the Brunel Award in 1998.
keyFeatures: Platform roof with some influence from Gothic architecture
funFacts: It closely resembles Calatrava's earlier Allen Lambert Galleria in Toronto.

name: Pavilhão do Conhecimento
aliases: Pavilhão do Conhecimento - Centro Ciência Viva

architects.name: João Luís Carrilho da Graça
architects.bio: Architect and lecturer born in Portalegre, who received the Pessoa Prize in 2008.

photos.alt: White stone building raised over a deep horizontal opening onto a paved courtyard with fountains
photos.credit: Photo: Leon · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Black corridor with a distorted chequerboard floor and a white arrow-like shape on the wall
photos.caption: A corridor.
photos.credit: Photo: GualdimG · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built for a world's fair in 1998, when it showed the relationship between people and the ocean.
It won the Valmor Prize in 1998.
Since 1999 it has been an interactive science centre.

summary.description: Designed by João Luís Carrilho da Graça with the engineer António Adão da Fonseca, the pavilion opened at Expo '98 as the 'Pavilion of the Knowledge of the Seas' and won the Valmor Prize in 1998. Remodelled after the fair, it reopened in July 1999 as the largest interactive science centre of Portugal's Ciência Viva network.
keyFeatures: Designed with engineer António Adão da Fonseca
funFacts: At Expo '98 it showed a full-size model of a submarine imagined by Leonardo da Vinci.

architects.name: Vittorio Gregotti
architects.bio: Architect born in Novara, seen as both a member of the Neo-Avant-Garde and a key figure in 1970s Postmodernism.

architects.name: Manuel Salgado
architects.bio: Lisbon architect who later led urban planning on Lisbon's city council from 2007 to 2019.

photos.alt: Long, nearly windowless walls of rough pinkish stone around a paved square
photos.credit: Photo: Alvesgaspar · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Concert hall with wooden ceiling slats and stone walls, an orchestra on stage before a full audience
photos.caption: The large auditorium.
photos.credit: Photo: Paulo Valdivieso · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built to host its country's first presidency of the European Council, in 1992.
It was designed and built in a very short time, between 1989 and 1992.
It is the largest building with cultural facilities in its country.

summary.description: Decided in January 1988 to host Portugal's Presidency of the European Council in 1992, the centre was built between 1989 and 1992 to designs by Vittorio Gregotti and Manuel Salgado, with interiors by Daciano Costa. Afterwards it became a permanent venue for conferences, exhibitions and the performing arts, with over 140,000 m² of usable space.
funFacts: By January 1992 three of its modules were ready for the EU presidency's institutions and security.

architects.name: Paulo Mendes da Rocha
architects.bio: Brazilian architect whose buildings, many in concrete, are associated with 'Brazilian Brutalism'; he worked almost exclusively in Brazil.

photos.alt: Long white box with a thin blue window strip, raised on round concrete columns over an open ground floor
photos.credit: Photo: Alejandro · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Long white hall with rows of historic carriages seen from above
photos.caption: The main hall.
photos.credit: Photo: Pedro Ribeiro Simões · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: The museum it houses was founded in 1905 by a queen, and was the first of its kind in the world.
Its collection was first shown in an 18th-century royal riding school across the road.
Its architect, from South America, designed it with a Lisbon studio; it opened in 2015.

summary.description: The National Coach Museum was created in 1905 by Queen Amélia in the old Royal Riding School of Belém. Its new building opposite, which houses most of the collection, is by the Brazilian architect Paulo Mendes da Rocha with the Ricardo Bak Gordon studio and the engineer Rui Furtado, and opened in 2015.
keyFeatures: New building opposite the old Royal Riding School
Collection of about 9,000 objects, including gala vehicles
funFacts: A 1944 hall for the old museum was designed by Raul Lino.

name: MAAT
aliases: Museu de Arte, Arquitetura e Tecnologia
Museum of Art, Architecture and Technology

architects.name: Amanda Levete
architects.bio: British architect and principal of AL_A; earlier, as a partner at Future Systems, she won the 1999 Stirling Prize.

photos.alt: Low, curving white building along a riverside promenade, seen from the water
photos.credit: Photo: Jakub Hałun · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Curving open gallery with a white floor under a dark ceiling grid
photos.caption: The oval gallery.
photos.credit: Photo: Dale Cruse · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It sits on a river to the west of its city centre, next to a former power station.
It cost about €20 million and is run by an energy company's foundation.
Its programme opened in June 2016.

summary.description: The museum of art, architecture and technology by Amanda Levete Architects stands on the Tagus west of Lisbon's centre. It connects to the Tejo Power Station, one of Portugal's most notable early 20th-century industrial buildings, and shows the EDP Foundation's collection. Its programme opened on 30 June 2016.
keyFeatures: Connection to the Tejo Power Station
Shows the EDP Foundation's art collection
funFacts: Its first four exhibitions were held in the renovated spaces of the old power station.

name: Terminal de Cruzeiros de Leixões
aliases: Terminal de Cruzeiros do Porto de Leixões

architects.name: Luís Pedro Silva
architects.bio: Portuguese architect whose design for this terminal won the international AZ Award in 2016.

photos.alt: Rounded white building wrapped in curving bands, with a dark glazed ground floor
photos.credit: Photo: Joseolgon · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Spiral ramp under a round skylight, its walls clad in white tiles
photos.caption: The spiral ramp.
photos.credit: Photo: Joseolgon · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was inaugurated in July 2015 to receive larger ships at a port near Porto.
Its spiral structure is clad in about a million white tiles made by a Portuguese porcelain firm.
It also houses a university marine research centre.

summary.description: Designed by Luís Pedro Silva and inaugurated in July 2015, the Leixões cruise terminal expanded the port's capacity for larger cruise ships. Its spiral structure is clad in around one million white tiles made by Vista Alegre, and it houses the University of Porto's Interdisciplinary Centre for Marine and Environmental Research (CIIMAR).
keyFeatures: About a million white Vista Alegre tiles
funFacts: It won the international AZ Award in 2016.
It was named one of the three best cruise ports in the world at the 2015 Seatrade Awards.

name: Pantheon
aliases: Basilica of St. Mary and the Martyrs

architects.name: Apollodorus of Damascus
architects.bio: Trajan's architect; on stylistic grounds some scholars see him as the designer of Hadrian's rebuilt temple, though the attribution is uncertain.

photos.alt: Round brick building with a deep portico of granite columns under a pediment, on a crowded square
photos.credit: Photo: Falk2 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Coffered concrete dome seen from below, with a round opening to the sky at its centre
photos.caption: The dome and oculus.
photos.credit: Photo: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It replaced an earlier temple built under Augustus; the emperor who rebuilt it kept the original founder's inscription.
Since 609 it has been a Catholic church.
Its height to the opening in the roof equals the diameter of its interior circle: 43 metres.

summary.description: Rebuilt by the emperor Hadrian on the site of Agrippa's temple and probably dedicated around AD 126, the Pantheon joins a portico of granite Corinthian columns to a round cella under a coffered dome of Roman concrete. Almost two thousand years later its dome is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.
keyFeatures: Portico with large granite Corinthian columns
Rotunda under a coffered concrete dome
Central oculus open to the sky
Equal height and interior diameter of 43 m
funFacts: The painter Raphael is buried inside.
Brunelleschi, among other architects, looked to it for inspiration.

architects.name: Unknown Roman architect
architects.bio: The designer of this Augustan provincial temple is not recorded; its form follows the Tuscan-style temple described by Vitruvius, but with the Corinthian order.

photos.alt: Small Roman temple with Corinthian columns on a high podium with steps, lit at night
photos.credit: Photo: Dennis G. Jarvis · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Coffered stone ceiling of the temple's porch, seen from below between columns
photos.caption: The porch ceiling.
photos.credit: Photo: Chatsam · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was dedicated or rededicated around AD 4–7 to two grandsons and heirs of Augustus who both died young.
Thomas Jefferson had a model of it made, and based the Virginia State Capitol on it.
It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2023.

summary.description: One of the best-preserved Roman temples anywhere, this mid-sized Augustan temple of the imperial cult stood over the forum of Roman Nîmes on a 2.85-metre podium. It was dedicated to Gaius and Lucius Caesar around AD 4–7. It later inspired the Église de la Madeleine in Paris and Jefferson's Virginia State Capitol.
keyFeatures: High podium with a frontal stair
Rectangle almost twice as long as wide
funFacts: Its dedicatory inscription was removed in the Middle Ages; its text is known from a reconstruction by Séguier.
The present door dates from 1824.

architects.name: The Hephaisteion Master
architects.bio: Many architects have been suggested, but without firm evidence the designer is simply called the Hephaisteion Master.

photos.alt: Complete Doric marble temple with a ring of columns, seen among shrubs
photos.credit: Photo: George E. Koronaios · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: View up between Doric columns and a sculpted frieze inside the colonnade
photos.caption: Inside the colonnade.
photos.credit: Photo: Marcok · CC BY-SA 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It stands on a hill at the north-west of an ancient city's agora.
For centuries it was wrongly believed to hold the remains of a hero, and named after him.
Begun in 449 BC, it was only roofed decades later, as funds went to a more famous temple nearby.

summary.description: This Doric peripteral temple to Hephaestus overlooks the Agora of Athens. Construction started in 449 BC, but workers and funds were diverted to the Parthenon, and its roof and cult statues were completed only around 421–415 BC. Used as the church of Saint George from the 7th century until 1834, it is one of the best-preserved Greek temples.
keyFeatures: Sculpted friezes in Pentelic and Parian marble
Pronaos aligned with the third flank columns
funFacts: In the 3rd century BC a garden of pomegranate, myrtle and laurel was planted around it.
It was long called the Theseion after Theseus.

architects.name: Unknown Roman architects
architects.bio: The builders of this imperial bath complex, erected under Septimius Severus and Caracalla, are not recorded.

photos.alt: Towering ruined brick walls and piers of a vast ancient building, on open grass
photos.credit: Photo: MatthiasKabel · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Ruined vaulted brick hall with a black-and-white mosaic floor
photos.caption: A hall with mosaic floor.
photos.credit: Photo: Sarahhoa · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was the second-largest public bath complex of its city, built in about AD 212–216.
Its central cold hall was copied for the main halls of Penn Station in New York and Chicago Union Station.
From 1937 to 1993 its hot room was the summer home of an opera company.

summary.description: Built between about AD 212 and 216 under Septimius Severus and Caracalla, the baths covered a central block of 214 by 110 metres and could hold some 1,600 bathers at once. A vaulted frigidarium, a tepidarium, a domed caldarium almost as wide as the Pantheon's dome and an open-air swimming pool lined the main axis. They worked until the 530s.
keyFeatures: Frigidarium under three groin vaults 32.9 m high
funFacts: The Farnese Bull and Farnese Hercules were found in its ruins.
Two of its granite tubs became fountains in Piazza Farnese.

architects.name: Julius Argentarius
architects.bio: A local banker and architect who sponsored the construction of the church, and also the nearby Sant'Apollinare in Classe.

photos.alt: Brick octagonal church with stepped roofs and arched windows, set in a garden
photos.credit: Photo: Commonists · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Lofty octagonal interior with arcades and gold mosaics in the apse
photos.caption: The octagon.
photos.credit: Photo: Gianni Careddu · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was begun in 526 by a local bishop and completed in 547, after the emperor Justinian conquered Italy.
Its plan is an octagon.
Its mosaics include famous portraits of an emperor and empress with their courts.

summary.description: Begun in 526 under Bishop Ecclesius and completed by Bishop Maximian in 547, San Vitale is the only major church from Justinian's reign to survive virtually intact. Its octagonal plan holds the largest and best-preserved Byzantine mosaics outside Istanbul, including the panels of Justinian and Theodora.
keyFeatures: Old Testament scenes in the lunettes
funFacts: Julius Argentarius may appear among the courtiers in the Justinian mosaic.

name: Chora Church
aliases: Church of the Holy Saviour in Chora

architects.name: Unknown Byzantine builders
architects.bio: The current fabric dates from 1077–1081, when Maria Doukaina rebuilt the church; the statesman Theodore Metochites added its mosaics, narthexes and funerary chapel in the 14th century.

photos.alt: Small brick-and-stone church with a dome and layered roofs, beside a lawn
photos.credit: Photo: Dosseman · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Marble-clad nave under a dome, with windows in its drum
photos.caption: The nave.
photos.credit: Photo: Bjelica · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was first built outside its city's walls, and later found itself inside new walls built in 413–414.
A statesman and scholar endowed its famous mosaics and frescoes around 1310–1321.
It has been a church, a mosque, a museum from 1945, and a mosque again since 2020.

summary.description: Rebuilt as an inscribed-cross church by Maria Doukaina in 1077–1081, the Chora was enriched between about 1310 and 1321 by Theodore Metochites, who added narthexes and a funerary chapel and paid for some of the finest surviving Late Byzantine mosaics and frescoes. They were left visible during most of its Ottoman use as a mosque.
funFacts: Theodore Metochites donated his personal library to the monastery.
He was exiled in 1328 by Andronicus III.

architects.name: Unknown chief architect
architects.bio: The name of the chief architect of the 11th-century church is not recorded; it was rebuilt under Doge Domenico I Contarini, modelled on the Church of the Holy Apostles in Constantinople.

photos.alt: Ornate church front with five arched portals, gilded mosaics and domes, across a paved square
photos.credit: Photo: Ekaterina Kuzmina · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Interior under gold-ground mosaic domes and vaults, with galleries and a marble floor
photos.caption: The domes and mosaics.
photos.credit: Photo: Nan Palmero · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was rebuilt from about 1063, on the model of a 6th-century church in Constantinople.
It was the private chapel of its republic's head of state until 1797.
Four ancient bronze horses, looted in the Fourth Crusade, stood over its entrance.

summary.description: The present church, begun probably in 1063 under Doge Domenico I Contarini and dedicated in 1094, took as its model the Church of the Holy Apostles in Constantinople, with a central plan crowned by domes. Over eight centuries its brick walls were clad in marble and its domes and vaults in gold-ground mosaics.
funFacts: It has been the cathedral of Venice only since 1807.
The Pala d'Oro was ordered from Constantinople in 1102.

architects.name: Unknown Byzantine builders
architects.bio: The builders of the monastery's two churches are not known; it grew around the tomb of the hermit Luke of Steiris.

photos.alt: Stone monastery churches with domes and a bell tower, in a valley below mountains
photos.credit: Photo: bradhostetler · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Stone church interior with arches and a marble column under a vault
photos.caption: The church.
photos.credit: Photo: bradhostetler · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It grew around the relics of a hermit who died in 953.
Its main church, tentatively dated to 1011–12, is the earliest surviving domed-octagon church.
It shares a UNESCO listing with two other Greek monasteries, Nea Moni and Daphni.

summary.description: Founded in the 10th century by the hermit Luke of Steiris near Distomo, the monastery has two joined churches: the Theotokos, the only church in mainland Greece known for certain to date from the 10th century, and the larger Katholikon of about 1011–12, the earliest domed-octagon church, with the best preserved mosaics of the Macedonian Renaissance.
keyFeatures: Dome on four squinches without a drum
funFacts: The saint's relics were said to exude a healing perfumed oil.

name: Chartres Cathedral
aliases: Cathedral of Our Lady of Chartres

architects.name: Unknown master masons
architects.bio: The architects of the 1194–1220 rebuilding are unknown; Jean Texier later added the Flamboyant north spire in 1507–1513.

photos.alt: Gothic cathedral with flying buttresses and a spire, floodlit at night
photos.credit: Photo: Rolf Kranz · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Tall Gothic nave looking towards a rose window above lancets
photos.caption: The nave and west rose.
photos.credit: Photo: Ludvig14 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was mostly built between 1194 and 1220, on the site of at least five earlier cathedrals.
Its two western spires are strikingly different: one plain, one Flamboyant.
Most of its original stained glass survives, and it guards a tunic said to have been worn by the Virgin Mary.

summary.description: Rebuilt mostly between 1194 and 1220 above earlier Romanesque basements, the cathedral is one of the most influential examples of High Gothic. Its experimental flying buttresses let the builders drop the gallery, narrow the triforium and enlarge the windows, most of which keep their original glass. UNESCO called it the high point of French Gothic art.
funFacts: During the Revolution a local committee planned to blow it up.
Its relic, the Sancta Camisa, still draws pilgrims.

architects.name: Unknown master mason
architects.bio: The design was once credited to Pierre de Montreuil; modern scholarship favours Jean de Chelles or Thomas de Cormont, or an unidentified master from Amiens.

photos.alt: Slender Gothic chapel with a spire and gables, rising behind palace buildings round a courtyard
photos.credit: Photo: Luisfff2812 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Upper chapel walled almost entirely with tall stained-glass windows under a blue starry vault
photos.caption: The upper chapel.
photos.credit: Photo: Pedro Szekely · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: A king built it to house relics including what was claimed to be Christ's Crown of Thorns.
It was consecrated on 26 April 1248 and has two superimposed chapels.
Its fifteen great windows form one of the largest collections of 13th-century stained glass.

summary.description: Built for Louis IX in the courtyard of the royal palace on the Île de la Cité and consecrated in 1248, the chapel housed his Passion relics. Its upper chapel is almost all glass: slender clustered supports and hidden iron chains carry fifteen great windows of the mid-13th century. It is a high point of Rayonnant Gothic.
keyFeatures: Hidden iron chains bracing the walls
Rose window added in the 15th century
funFacts: The relics were later moved to Notre-Dame.
The present cedar spire was built from 1852.

name: Durham Cathedral
aliases: Cathedral Church of Christ, Blessed Mary the Virgin and St Cuthbert of Durham

architects.name: William de St-Calais
architects.bio: Bishop of Durham who demolished the old Saxon church and laid the foundation stone of the new cathedral on 11 August 1093; the cathedral was designed and built under him.

photos.alt: Massive Romanesque cathedral with square towers above wooded riverbanks
photos.credit: Photo: Benjamin Smith · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Nave vault of pointed stone ribs seen from below
photos.caption: The nave vault.
photos.credit: Photo: Benjamin Smith · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It holds the shrines of the saints Cuthbert and Bede.
Most of the present building was completed between 1093 and 1133.
Its nave ceiling is the earliest surviving example of a pointed rib vault.

summary.description: Begun in 1093 under Bishop William de St-Calais and largely complete by 1133, the cathedral is the largest and most perfect Norman building in England, according to UNESCO. Its nave holds the earliest surviving pointed rib vault, a turning point that anticipated the Gothic of northern France.
keyFeatures: Pointed rib vault over the nave
funFacts: During the Wars of the Three Kingdoms it held 3,000 Scottish prisoners, 1,700 of whom died there.
It has stood in for fantasy locations in films.

architects.name: Buscheto
architects.bio: Architect who began the cathedral in 1064 and welcomed Islamic and Armenian influence; his tomb is beside the north door of the façade.

architects.name: Rainaldo
architects.bio: Architect who lengthened the nave, enlarged the transept and designed the marble façade in the 12th century.

photos.alt: Marble Romanesque cathedral with tiers of arcades and a dome, beside a lawn
photos.credit: Photo: kallerna · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Nave of striped marble columns and arches under a gilded coffered ceiling
photos.caption: The nave.
photos.credit: Photo: Eric Kilby · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was paid for with spoils from fighting in Sicily in 1064.
It is the oldest of three famous buildings on its square, one of which leans.
Its black-and-white marble, raised arches and elliptical dome recall the great mosques.

summary.description: Begun in 1064 by Buscheto and consecrated in 1118, the cathedral defines Pisan Romanesque. Rainaldo lengthened it and built the façade of grey and white marble with four tiers of loggias. Inside, striped marble, raised lancet arches and an elliptical dome create an effect compared to the great mosques.
keyFeatures: Façade with four tiers of loggias
funFacts: Its roof was replaced after a fire in 1595.
Its bronze spoils of war included the Pisa Griffin; a copy is there now.

architects.name: Sedefkar Mehmed Agha
architects.bio: A pupil of Sinan from Elbasan who synthesised his master's ideas, aiming for overwhelming size, majesty and splendour; his biographer called the mosque the culmination of his career.

photos.alt: Mosque with a cascade of domes and six slender minarets, seen across a park with palm trees
photos.credit: Photo: kallerna · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Prayer hall under great domes on massive piers, lit by hanging rings of lamps
photos.caption: The prayer hall.
photos.credit: Photo: Julian Lupyan · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built between 1609 and 1617, on the side of an old Byzantine hippodrome.
It is flanked by six minarets.
Thousands of tiles and painted floral motifs in mostly blue colours give it its popular name.

summary.description: Built for Sultan Ahmed I between 1609 and 1617 next to the old Hippodrome and facing the Hagia Sophia, the mosque was probably meant to rival that great church. Its architect Sedefkar Mehmed Agha based the design on Sinan's Şehzade Mosque. A large courtyard precedes the prayer hall, whose thousands of Iznik tiles give the building its popular name.
keyFeatures: Large courtyard before the prayer hall
funFacts: Some of its inscriptions give the year 1616, although the opening ceremony was in 1617.

architects.name: Mimar Sinan
architects.bio: Chief architect to the Ottoman sultans for some fifty years, Sinan was also an engineer and mathematician, and his mosques defined classical Ottoman architecture.

photos.alt: Great domed mosque framed by tall minarets, seen past a stone wall
photos.credit: Photo: Dosseman · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Vast domed prayer hall ringed by arcades and galleries, with a ring of lamps
photos.caption: The prayer hall.
photos.credit: Photo: İhsan Deniz Kılıçoğlu · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was commissioned by Sultan Selim II and built between 1568 and 1575.
Its architect considered it his masterpiece.
Its courtyard, ringed by porticos of arches and domes, frames the view of one huge central dome.

summary.description: Commissioned by Selim II and built by Mimar Sinan between 1568 and 1575, the mosque is regarded as Sinan's crowning masterpiece and one of the highest achievements of Islamic architecture. Its courtyard, surrounded by porticos of arches and domes, frames the approach to the huge central dome.
keyFeatures: Courtyard with porticos of arches and domes
Fluted dome before the prayer-hall entrance
funFacts: Sinan himself repaired it in 1584 after lightning damage.
Its dome was damaged by artillery during the siege of 1913.

architects.name: Mimar Sinan
architects.bio: Chief architect to the Ottoman sultans for some fifty years, Sinan was also an engineer and mathematician, and his mosques defined classical Ottoman architecture.

photos.alt: Lead-covered dome and semi-domes of a stone mosque with a minaret, against a blue sky
photos.credit: Photo: Dosseman · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Prayer hall with walls covered in blue and red floral tiles
photos.caption: The prayer hall.
photos.credit: Photo: Dosseman · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It is named after a grand vizier who was married to the sultan's daughter.
It stands in a market district, near a famous spice bazaar.
Almost every vertical surface inside, and under the porch, is covered in many designs of Iznik tiles.

summary.description: Designed by Mimar Sinan for the Grand Vizier Rüstem Pasha, husband of Suleiman's daughter Mihrimah Sultan, the mosque was probably built between 1561 and 1563 in the Tahtakale market district. It is unique among Sinan's mosques for its lavishly tiled interior, covered in many different Iznik designs.
keyFeatures: Iznik tiles on almost every vertical surface
funFacts: Rüstem Pasha may have ordered the tiles to support the court designer Kara Memi.

architects.name: Acem Ali
architects.bio: The chief architect of the palace in its early period.

architects.name: Mimar Sinan
architects.bio: Chief architect to the Ottoman sultans for some fifty years, Sinan was also an engineer and mathematician, and his mosques defined classical Ottoman architecture.

photos.alt: Long arcaded pavilion with a deep roof overhang, beside a garden courtyard
photos.credit: Photo: Joseolgon · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Tiled passage with arches, hanging lamps and a gilded gate
photos.caption: Inside the palace.
photos.credit: Photo: Julian Lupyan · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Its construction began in 1459, six years after the conquest of its city.
It was the main residence of its empire's rulers until the move to a newer palace on the Bosphorus.
It is organised around four main courtyards and became a museum in 1924.

summary.description: Ordered by Mehmed the Conqueror and built from 1459, the palace was the administrative centre of the Ottoman Empire and the sultans' main residence until the court moved to Dolmabahçe in 1856. Four main courtyards and many smaller buildings include the Harem and the Imperial Council. Mimar Sinan rebuilt parts after a fire in 1574.
keyFeatures: Kitchens with two rows of 20 chimneys by Sinan
Pavilions and kiosks of later centuries
funFacts: Its name means Cannon Gate and was given in the 19th century.
Its treasury displays the Spoonmaker's Diamond and the Topkapı Dagger.

architects.name: Diogo de Boitaca
architects.bio: An architect and engineer of unknown origin who pioneered the Manueline style at the Monastery of Jesus in Setúbal and drew the first plans of the Jerónimos Monastery in Lisbon.

architects.name: Nicolau Chanterene
architects.bio: Sculptor and architect who built the main portal in 1522–1525 and carved the royal tombs placed in the chancel in 1530.

photos.alt: Ornate pale stone church front with pinnacles and a carved portal, above a square with a fountain
photos.credit: Photo: Berthold Werner · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Nave under a ribbed vault, with blue tile panels, a gilded pulpit and a gilded altarpiece
photos.caption: The church.
photos.credit: Photo: ほっきー · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was founded in 1131 and was the most important monastery of the early kingdom.
The first two kings of its country are buried in its chancel.
It was completely renovated in the early 16th century by order of King Manuel I.

summary.description: Founded in 1131 outside the walls of Coimbra, the monastery holds the tombs of Afonso Henriques and Sancho I, and so was granted the status of National Pantheon. King Manuel I had it renovated in the early 16th century: Diogo de Boitaca laid out the Manueline church and chapter house, and Nicolau Chanterene built the portal and the royal tombs.
keyFeatures: Tombs of the first two kings, rearranged in 1530
funFacts: Its scriptorium helped Afonso Henriques consolidate royal power.

architects.name: Unknown royal builders
architects.bio: The palace grew in campaigns sponsored by King John I from around 1415 and by King Manuel I between 1497 and 1530; its master builders are not recorded.

photos.alt: Two huge white conical chimneys rising above a palace wing with Moorish-style windows
photos.credit: Photo: Vitor Oliveira · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Palace room with a wooden ceiling, a chandelier, red doors and a lacquered screen
photos.caption: A palace room.
photos.credit: Photo: Vitor Oliveira · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It is the best-preserved medieval royal residence in its country, lived in from the early 15th century to the late 19th.
Two enormous conical chimneys rise above its kitchens.
One room is painted with magpies holding the motto 'por bem', after a king was caught kissing a lady-in-waiting.

summary.description: Much of the palace dates from John I's campaign from around 1415; Manuel I added a wing with Manueline windows between 1497 and 1530 and redecorated rooms with azulejos made for him in Seville. Its blend of Gothic, Manueline, Moorish and Mudéjar styles includes the Coat of Arms Room, one of Europe's most important heraldic rooms.
keyFeatures: Pair of giant conical kitchen chimneys
funFacts: King John II was acclaimed king here.
The Swan Room is named after the swans painted on its ceiling.

name: Sé do Funchal
aliases: Cathedral of Our Lady of the Assumption

architects.name: Pêro Anes
architects.bio: A royal carpenter who replaced the first master builder, João Gonçalves, introducing advanced methods from the mainland.

photos.alt: White church with dark stone edges, a rose window and a pointed portal, beside a square bell tower
photos.credit: Photo: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Gilded chancel under a carved and painted wooden ceiling
photos.caption: The chancel.
photos.credit: Photo: Holger Uwe Schmitt · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It stands on an Atlantic island and was begun in 1486 under the duke who later became King Manuel I.
It was raised to cathedral status by a papal bull in 1514.
Its roof is a Mudéjar-inspired design in cedar wood.

summary.description: Begun in 1486 under the future Manuel I and structurally complete in 1514, the cathedral of Funchal is one of the few buildings that survives virtually intact from the early colonisation of Madeira. Its Gothic and Manueline design is crowned inside by a Mudéjar-inspired cedar roof, and its main altar was consecrated by 1517.
funFacts: Manuel I gave it a silver processional cross, a masterpiece of Manueline silverwork.

name: Igreja Matriz da Golegã
aliases: Igreja de Nossa Senhora da Conceição (Golegã)

architects.name: Diogo de Boitaca
architects.bio: An architect and engineer of unknown origin who pioneered the Manueline style at the Monastery of Jesus in Setúbal and drew the first plans of the Jerónimos Monastery in Lisbon.

photos.alt: White church with an elaborately carved stone portal and a tall tower with a pointed spire
photos.credit: Photo: Vitor Oliveira · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Nave with timber roof leading to a ribbed Gothic chancel arch and tiled chapel
photos.caption: The nave.
photos.credit: Photo: Threeohsix · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built in the first half of the 16th century, replacing a small Gothic parish church.
A king's frequent stays in a nearby town favoured its construction.
Its carved portal is one of the most emblematic examples of its style.

summary.description: Built in the first half of the 16th century to replace a small Gothic church, the parish church of Golegã is one of the best-preserved examples of the Manueline style, with a magnificent portal. The royal architect Diogo Boitaca probably intervened in its construction; by 1530 its chancel was already used for burials. Restorations in the 1930s and 1940s recovered its Manueline appearance.
keyFeatures: Bell tower with a tall prismatic spire
Gothic inscription held by angels at the portal
funFacts: In the 18th century a storey and a dome were added to its tower.

architects.name: Leon Battista Alberti
architects.bio: Humanist author and architect of the early Renaissance, a theorist of architecture whose churches elaborated the triumphal-arch motif.

photos.alt: Church front shaped like a triumphal arch with pilasters and a pediment, beside a Gothic bell tower
photos.credit: Photo: Sailko · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Single great nave under a painted barrel vault, with side chapels and a domed crossing
photos.caption: The nave.
photos.credit: Photo: PierangeloGatto · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was begun in 1472, the year its architect died, for a ruling marquess.
Its façade and interior both elaborate the motif of a triumphal arch.
It was built to receive pilgrims who come to see a vial said to contain the Blood of Christ.

summary.description: Commissioned by Ludovico III Gonzaga, the church was begun in 1472 to designs by Leon Battista Alberti. He broke with the basilican tradition by opening chapels off a single nave instead of aisles, and made the façade and interior echo the triumphal arch. Its dome, by Filippo Juvarra, was added only in 1732–1782.
funFacts: The painter Andrea Mantegna is buried in one of its chapels.
Its bell tower (1414) survives from an earlier monastery.

architects.name: Domenico da Cortona
architects.bio: The Tuscan architect to whom the original design is attributed, with doubts; his wooden model survived long enough to be drawn in the 17th century.

photos.alt: Huge white château with round towers and a crowded roofscape, reflected in still water
photos.credit: Photo: Arnaud Scherer · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Twisting stone staircase with an open central core seen through arched openings
photos.caption: The double-spiral staircase.
photos.credit: Photo: Eric Kilby · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built between 1519 and 1547 as a hunting lodge for a king, who stayed there barely seven weeks.
It has 440 rooms, 282 fireplaces and 84 staircases.
Its central double-spiral staircase is sometimes credited to Leonardo da Vinci, though this is unconfirmed.

summary.description: Commissioned by Francis I and built between 1519 and 1547, Chambord is the largest château of the Loire Valley. Its design is attributed to Domenico da Cortona, with possible influence from Leonardo da Vinci. Rooms are grouped into self-contained suites around a central open double-spiral staircase, and its roofscape of towers and chimneys looks like the skyline of a town.
keyFeatures: Roofscape of towers, lanterns and chimneys
funFacts: Henry James said its roof looked more like the spires of a city than a single building.
Its furnishings were sold off in 1792.

name: El Escorial
aliases: Monastery of San Lorenzo de El Escorial
Real Sitio de San Lorenzo de El Escorial

architects.name: Juan Bautista de Toledo
architects.bio: Architect-royal from 1559 who designed the complex with Philip II and oversaw it until his death.

architects.name: Juan de Herrera
architects.bio: Toledo's apprentice, generally regarded as the architect of the Escorial, who completed it in 1584.

photos.alt: Vast austere granite building with a corner tower and spire under a blue sky
photos.credit: Photo: FrDr · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Long library hall with carved bookcases, a marble floor and a frescoed barrel vault
photos.caption: The library.
photos.credit: Photo: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built between 1563 and 1584 by order of a king, and is the largest Renaissance building in the world.
It combines a monastery, basilica, royal palace, pantheon and library.
Its library was the first in Europe to set bookcases along the walls.

summary.description: Built for Philip II between 1563 and 1584, El Escorial was designed by Juan Bautista de Toledo and completed by Juan de Herrera. Philip asked for 'simplicity in the construction, severity in the whole'. The grid-like complex holds a monastery, a Greek-cross basilica, the king's palace, the royal pantheon and a library of more than 40,000 volumes.
keyFeatures: Greek-cross basilica with a great dome
Library hall 54 m long with frescoed vault
funFacts: Domenico Fontana drew on its library for the Vatican Library.
A fire in 1671 destroyed about 5,280 manuscripts.

architects.name: Michelangelo
architects.bio: Florentine sculptor, painter and architect; his library design here is one of his most important architectural achievements and an example of Mannerism.

photos.alt: Plain stone building with a small dome, rising behind a cloister wall on a narrow street
photos.credit: Photo: sailko · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Long reading room with rows of carved wooden desks under a coffered timber ceiling
photos.caption: The reading room.
photos.credit: Photo: Angela Stefanoni · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built in a church cloister under the patronage of a Medici pope.
Its vestibule is filled by a staircase that seems to pour down from the upper level.
Its architect left the city in 1534, and others finished it from his instructions; it opened by 1571.

summary.description: Commissioned in 1523 by the Medici pope Clement VII and built in a cloister of San Lorenzo, the library was designed by Michelangelo. When he left Florence in 1534 only the reading-room walls were done; Tribolo, Vasari and Ammannati completed it from his plans. Its tall vestibule with a flowing staircase is a key work of Mannerism.
funFacts: Mark Rothko said the vestibule influenced his Seagram murals.
Its core collection is about 3,000 manuscripts.

architects.name: Louis Le Vau
architects.bio: Court architect from 1654, whose work at Vaux-le-Vicomte impressed Louis XIV; he wrapped Louis XIII's château in the 'enveloppe' from 1668.

architects.name: Jules Hardouin-Mansart
architects.bio: First Architect to Louis XIV from 1678, who added the Hall of Mirrors, the great wings and the palace chapel.

photos.alt: Very long palace façade seen from the end of a formal garden terrace
photos.credit: Photo: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Long gallery lined with mirrors and windows under crystal chandeliers, crowded with visitors
photos.caption: The Hall of Mirrors.
photos.credit: Photo: dave one · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It began as a king's modest brick-and-stone hunting lodge built in 1623.
The court and the royal government lived there permanently from 1682 until October 1789.
The German Empire was proclaimed in its most famous gallery in 1871.

summary.description: Louis XIV turned his father's hunting lodge into the seat of the French court. From 1668 Louis Le Vau encased the old château, while André Le Nôtre laid out the gardens; from 1678 Jules Hardouin-Mansart added the Hall of Mirrors, vast wings and finally the chapel (1699–1710). It holds roughly 2,300 rooms.
keyFeatures: Le Vau's 'enveloppe' around the old château
funFacts: The Hall of Mirrors became a military hospital at one point.
About 1,000 of its rooms belong to a national history museum.

name: San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane
aliases: Saint Charles at the Four Fountains

architects.name: Francesco Borromini
architects.bio: Baroque architect whose first independent commission this was; he offered to do it free of charge to start his solo career.

photos.alt: Narrow church front of undulating concave and convex bays with columns, niches and statues
photos.credit: Photo: Chabe01 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Oval dome with deep coffers of crosses, octagons and hexagons, lit from a lantern
photos.caption: The dome.
photos.credit: Photo: Bradley Weber · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built for a religious order dedicated to freeing Christian slaves.
It was its architect's first independent commission; he offered to do it for free.
Its upper façade, with serpentine curves, was completed only after the architect's death.

summary.description: Built for the Spanish Trinitarians on the Quirinal Hill, the church was Francesco Borromini's first independent commission. The church was built in 1638–1641 and dedicated in 1646 to Saint Charles Borromeo; its serpentine façade was finished by his nephew Bernardo, with work continuing until 1682. It is an iconic masterpiece of Baroque architecture.
keyFeatures: Monastic complex on the Quirinal Hill
Living quarters and library designed first, from 1634
funFacts: Bernini's oval church of Sant'Andrea al Quirinale stands further along the same street.

architects.name: Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach
architects.bio: Won the competition for the church against Galli-Bibiena and Hildebrandt; after his death his son Joseph Emanuel completed it.

photos.alt: Domed church with a temple portico flanked by two great carved columns
photos.credit: Photo: Nick Savchenko · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Frescoed oval dome seen from inside its drum
photos.caption: The dome.
photos.credit: Photo: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: An emperor vowed to build it in 1713, a year after his city's last great plague.
It is dedicated to a saint revered as a healer of plague sufferers, the emperor's namesake.
Two columns inspired by Trajan's Column flank its entrance.

summary.description: Charles VI pledged the church in 1713, after Vienna's last major plague, to his patron saint Charles Borromeo. Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach won the competition; building began in 1716 and his son Joseph Emanuel completed it in 1737. It unites a temple portico, two columns modelled on Trajan's Column and a dome on a high drum.
keyFeatures: Two spiral-relief columns by Lorenzo Mattielli
funFacts: Its iconographic programme was devised by the imperial official Carl Gustav Heraeus.

architects.name: Jakob Prandtauer
architects.bio: Architect to whose designs today's Baroque abbey was built between 1702 and 1736.

photos.alt: Long yellow abbey with a domed church and twin towers on a rocky height
photos.credit: Photo: Tournasol7 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Library with gilded bookcases, marquetry floor and a painted ceiling
photos.caption: The library.
photos.credit: Photo: Rollroboter · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It stands on a rocky outcrop above a great river, at the start of the Wachau valley.
Its community was founded in 1089, when a margrave gave one of his castles to monks.
Its present building dates from 1702–1736, and its library has been famed since the Middle Ages.

summary.description: Founded in 1089 when Margrave Leopold II gave a castle to Benedictine monks, the abbey overlooks the Danube from a rocky outcrop. Today's Baroque abbey was built between 1702 and 1736 to designs by Jakob Prandtauer; its church holds frescoes by Johann Michael Rottmayr and Paul Troger.
keyFeatures: Domed abbey church with twin towers
Site on a rock above the Danube
funFacts: Its fame let it escape the dissolutions under Emperor Joseph II.

architects.name: Jacques-Germain Soufflot
architects.bio: Architect of the building for Louis XV; he did not live to see it completed, but his remains were moved inside in 1829.

photos.alt: Domed Neoclassical building with a Corinthian portico, across a square
photos.credit: Photo: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Coffered vaults and a painted apse mosaic seen between Corinthian columns
photos.caption: The interior.
photos.credit: Photo: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built for a king who vowed in 1744 to replace a church if he recovered from illness.
During the Revolution it was turned into a mausoleum for distinguished citizens.
In 1851 a physicist hung a pendulum from its dome to demonstrate the Earth's rotation.

summary.description: Built between 1758 and 1790 to designs by Jacques-Germain Soufflot, the church of Saint Genevieve was transformed in 1791 into a mausoleum for great French citizens, modelled on the Pantheon in Rome. It was twice returned to church use before becoming exclusively a mausoleum in 1881.
keyFeatures: Mausoleum modelled on the Pantheon in Rome
funFacts: A copy of Foucault's pendulum still hangs there.
Neither Soufflot nor Louis XV lived to see it finished.

architects.name: Karl Friedrich Schinkel
architects.bio: Architect charged by Frederick William III with planning a public museum for the royal art collection, as part of an ensemble around the Lustgarten.

photos.alt: Long colonnade of Ionic columns along a wall painted with red panels
photos.caption: The colonnade.
photos.credit: Photo: Dr. Zeltsam · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Domed rotunda ringed by columns and statues, with a patterned floor
photos.caption: The rotunda.
photos.credit: Photo: Dr. Zeltsam · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built as a public museum for a royal art collection, reflecting the Humboldtian ideal of education.
Its front of eighteen Ionic columns faces a pleasure garden.
It was inaugurated on 3 August 1830.

summary.description: Built between 1825 and 1830 for King Frederick William III to plans by Karl Friedrich Schinkel, the museum is a major work of German Neoclassicism. A long hall of eighteen Ionic columns faces the Lustgarten, and inside a domed rotunda recalls Classical antiquity.
funFacts: The crown prince sent Schinkel a pencil sketch of a hall with a classical portico.

architects.name: Robert Smirke
architects.bio: Neoclassical architect asked to plan an eastern extension; his building replaced Montagu House over the following decades.

photos.alt: Row of tall Ionic columns of a Greek Revival portico above wet steps
photos.credit: Photo: Dale Cruse · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Long gallery with tall bookcases and display cases under a decorated ceiling
photos.caption: The King's Library gallery.
photos.credit: Photo: Dale Cruse · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It opened to the public in 1759 in a converted 17th-century mansion on the same site.
Work on its present building began in 1823 with a gallery for a king's library.
Its central courtyard was roofed over in glass in 2000.

summary.description: Founded in 1753 and opened in Montagu House in 1759, the museum was rebuilt to Robert Smirke's Greek Revival plan from 1823, beginning with the King's Library Gallery; the opening of the forecourt in 1852 completed the plan. In 2000 the central quadrangle became the glass-roofed Great Court, the largest covered square in Europe.
funFacts: From 1825 to 1850 it was the largest building site in Europe.

name: La Madeleine
aliases: Church of St Mary Magdalene, Paris

architects.name: Pierre-Alexandre Vignon
architects.bio: Architect personally chosen by Napoleon over the Academy's candidate, with a design modelled on an ancient temple.

photos.alt: Corner of a temple-like building with a pediment over rows of Corinthian columns
photos.credit: Photo: Guilhem Vellut · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Marble high altar with a sculpted group of angels and gilded candlesticks
photos.caption: The high altar.
photos.credit: Photo: Manley75 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Its first stone was dedicated in 1764 by a king, but the Revolution halted the work.
An emperor declared in 1806 that it would become a temple to the glory of his army.
It is surrounded on all four sides by Corinthian columns and was completed as a church in 1842.

summary.description: Begun under Louis XV, the church was redesigned for Napoleon in 1806 by Pierre-Alexandre Vignon as a temple to the glory of the Grande Armée, modelled on ancient temples. After Napoleon's fall it became a church again, completed in 1842. Corinthian columns surround it on all four sides.
keyFeatures: Corinthian columns on all four sides
Design modelled on an ancient Greek or Roman temple
funFacts: It was once proposed as a railway station.

architects.name: Charles Barry
architects.bio: Won the competition to design the new palace after the fire of 1834, choosing the Gothic Revival style.

architects.name: Augustus Pugin
architects.bio: Barry's assistant on the new Gothic Revival palace; both men died before it was finished.

photos.alt: Long Gothic Revival palace with towers along a river, seen from the water
photos.credit: Photo: Mike Peel · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Octagonal Gothic hall with tiled floor, statues, tall windows and a great chandelier
photos.caption: The Central Lobby.
photos.credit: Photo: Jorge Royan · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: A fire in 1834, started by an overheated stove burning tally sticks, destroyed most of its predecessor.
Construction started in 1840 and lasted about 30 years.
Its clock tower houses a bell with a famous nickname.

summary.description: After the fire of 1834, Charles Barry won the competition for a new palace in the Gothic Revival style, incorporating the surviving 11th-century Westminster Hall. Built from 1840 over about 30 years, with Augustus Pugin as Barry's assistant, it spread the Gothic Revival far beyond Britain.
funFacts: Both Barry and Pugin died before it was finished.
It has been part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987.

architects.name: Eduard Riedel
architects.bio: Architect who realised the castle on the basis of drafts by the stage designer Christian Jank.

architects.name: Christian Jank
architects.bio: Stage designer and scenic painter who drafted the castle's design, drawing on theatre scenery.

photos.alt: White castle with turrets on a forested crag, above a wide plain
photos.credit: Photo: Sergiy Galyonkin · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Old photograph of an ornate room with carved wood and painted walls
photos.caption: A room, historical photograph.
photos.credit: Photo: Unknown photographer · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built from 1869 for a king, paid from his personal fortune and borrowing rather than public funds.
Its design drew on stage scenery and evokes operas such as Tannhäuser and Lohengrin.
The king died in 1886 and it opened to the public shortly afterwards, still unfinished.

summary.description: Ludwig II of Bavaria had the three-winged castle built from 1869 in a Neo-Romanesque style, to plans realised by Eduard Riedel from drafts by the stage designer Christian Jank. Theatre themes run through it, recalling operas such as Tannhäuser and Lohengrin. The king moved into the unfinished palace in 1884 and died in 1886.
keyFeatures: Neo-Romanesque forms mixed with Gothic and Byzantine decoration
Throne Hall with a steel framework
Site on a crag above Hohenschwangau
funFacts: It was called New Hohenschwangau Castle until after Ludwig's death.
It became part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2025.

architects.name: Pierre Cuypers
architects.bio: Architect who won the second competition, in 1876, for the museum's new building.

photos.alt: Large red-brick museum with steep-roofed towers and an arched passage, behind flower boxes
photos.credit: Photo: Mustang Joe · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Gallery with patterned walls and arches, crowded with visitors before a large dark painting
photos.caption: A main gallery.
photos.credit: Photo: Hnapel · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: The national museum it houses was founded in The Hague in 1798 and moved in 1808.
Its architect won a second competition in 1876, having come second in the first.
Its new building opened on 13 July 1885.

summary.description: After a first competition failed, Pierre Cuypers won the 1876 contest for the national museum's new building. Construction began on 1 October 1876 and the museum opened on 13 July 1885, bringing together collections that include Rembrandt's Night Watch.
funFacts: King Louis Bonaparte, Napoleon's brother, moved the museum to Amsterdam in 1808.

architects.name: William Henry Barlow
architects.bio: Engineer who designed the passenger station, with wrought-iron pillars supporting a single-span roof.

architects.name: George Gilbert Scott
architects.bio: Won the competition for the Midland Grand Hotel on the station's front, with an ornate Gothic red-brick scheme.

photos.alt: Ornate red-brick Gothic hotel front with towers and pointed windows
photos.credit: Photo: Wei-Te Wong · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Vast arched iron-and-glass train shed with a long platform
photos.caption: The train shed.
photos.credit: Photo: Colin · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It opened on 1 October 1868 on the site of a slum called Agar Town.
A poet laureate led the campaign that saved it from demolition.
Since 2007 it has been the terminus for international trains through the Channel Tunnel.

summary.description: The station, designed by William Henry Barlow, opened in 1868 with a single-span roof on wrought-iron pillars, raised 5 metres above the street. George Gilbert Scott's Midland Grand Hotel forms its ornate Gothic front. Saved by a campaign led by John Betjeman, it was refurbished for High Speed 1 and reopened in 2007.
funFacts: It received Grade I listing just 10 days before demolition was due to begin.
